preferences.everyday_problem: The problem is that before we talk about strategy, we need a way to say what one person is trying to get. A person may like one outcome more than another even when dollars, risk, effort, and timing are mixed together.
preferences.first_principles_reason: This exists because choice needs ordering. If the person cannot rank outcomes, then words like better, worse, rational, or optimal have nothing to attach to.
preferences.mathematical_object: The object is a preference relation: a comparison rule over outcomes. When it is complete the person can compare any two outcomes; when it is transitive the comparisons do not cycle back on themselves.
preferences.operation: List the possible outcomes, ask which ones the person ranks above which others, and then check whether those rankings are consistent enough to be represented and used in a model.
preferences.worked_mini_example: If someone prefers coffee to tea and tea to water, transitivity says they should prefer coffee to water. Without that, a model can chase its own tail because the person can be walked around a cycle of choices.
preferences.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to think preferences are emotions. In the course they are a disciplined choice ordering, not a psychological biography.
preferences.recognize_in_new_work: Look for the place where an economic model has to say what an actor counts as better before any strategic reasoning begins.
preferences.why_it_matters: Preferences matter because they are the first act of compression in the course. The model cannot carry every emotional, legal, or social detail of an outcome, so it keeps the order of what the player would choose. That order becomes the base layer for utility, payoffs, and later welfare comparisons.
preferences.what_breaks_without_it: Without preferences, a payoff table has no disciplined source. The analyst could assign numbers, but there would be no explanation of why a player ranks one result over another or why a later best-response calculation should be trusted.
preferences.naive_problem: A naive reading says people just choose what they like. The course needs more: liking has to be stable enough that the model can compare outcomes across cases without changing the meaning of better halfway through the argument.
preferences.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when choices form cycles or depend on irrelevant framing. If a person prefers A to B, B to C, and C to A, the model cannot build a coherent choice rule from that ordering.
preferences.lecture_emphasis: The preference lecture is doing groundwork. It is not yet solving games; it is making sure later payoff numbers stand for a choice ranking rather than for an unexplained scoreboard.
preferences.cross_course_connections: Preferences feed utility, expected utility, bargaining surplus, bidder values, and welfare comparisons. The same primitive is quiet in later lectures because the course has already installed it as the language of individual motivation.
preferences.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version starts with a simple pressure: people choose among outcomes before any game begins. The course therefore needs a relation that says whether one outcome is ranked above, below, or tied with another. Completeness means the model can compare the relevant outcomes; transitivity means the comparisons do not cycle. Those assumptions are not moral truths about people. They are the minimum structure needed to turn choice into an object that can be used later. Once that object exists, utility can represent it numerically, and payoff tables can inherit the ranking.
preferences.mathematical_intuition: The math is a compression of choice behavior. Instead of carrying the full story of each outcome, the preference relation keeps the ordering that matters for the decision. If x is preferred to y, a utility representation can assign x a higher number than y. The number is secondary; the preserved order is the point.
preferences.student_trap: Students often get stuck by asking whether the preference is realistic for every human mood. The course is doing a modeling move: it asks whether the relevant choices in the problem can be treated as stable enough for strategic analysis.
preferences.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because ordinary language can hide contradictions. People can say they like many things, but a model needs to know whether those comparisons can be used together. A preference relation is the smallest formal object that lets the course ask whether the choices are complete enough and consistent enough to support later payoff reasoning.
preferences.course_boundary_note: The boundary is that preferences describe rankings within the modeled choice problem; they do not explain where desires come from. If the lecture question is about persuasion, learning, or changing tastes, preference is only the starting input, not the full explanation.

utility.everyday_problem: The problem is that rankings are awkward to compute with. A payoff table, expected value, or equilibrium check needs numbers, not only verbal statements like this outcome is preferred.
utility.first_principles_reason: Utility exists because mathematics needs a handle. If rankings can be represented by numbers, then comparison, maximization, and averaging become possible.
utility.mathematical_object: The object is a utility function u that assigns a number to each outcome while preserving the preference ordering. Higher utility means higher in the ranking, not necessarily more money or happiness.
utility.operation: Choose numbers that preserve the ordering, then use those numbers in payoff tables or expected-utility calculations.
utility.worked_mini_example: If a diner ranks pizza above salad above soup, utilities 10, 5, and 0 work just as well as 100, 20, and -7 for ordinary choice. The numbers carry the order; their absolute size is not the point unless risk is involved.
utility.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat utility units as physical units like inches. Utility usually represents order, and only specific setups justify stronger numerical claims.
utility.recognize_in_new_work: Look for a paper turning goals, payoffs, welfare, or preferences into a number that can be compared or optimized.
utility.why_it_matters: Utility matters because it lets the course calculate with preferences. Once rankings are represented by numbers, the model can compare payoffs inside matrices, trees, lotteries, auctions, and bargaining problems without pretending the numbers are literal units of happiness.
utility.what_breaks_without_it: Without utility, later algebra would float free from choice behavior. The course could say one outcome is preferred, but it could not easily compute expected payoffs, best responses, or surplus divisions.
utility.naive_problem: A naive reading treats utility as a psychological fuel gauge. The better first-principles reading is that utility is a representation: it preserves the ranking needed for the question being asked.
utility.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when students compare utility numbers across people or across transformations as if the scale were physical. Many game-theory results need the ordering or expected ranking, not interpersonal happiness units.
utility.lecture_emphasis: The lecture emphasizes why the number is useful and limited at the same time. It turns preference into something computable while keeping the interpretation tied to choice.
utility.cross_course_connections: Utility becomes the payoff entry in strategic-form games, the continuation value in trees, the expected payoff in Bayesian games, and the private value in auctions. It is the bridge from wanting to calculating.
utility.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version treats utility as a translation layer. The course starts with preference, which is qualitative, then introduces a number so that comparisons can be computed. A utility function lets payoff matrices, trees, and expected values use arithmetic while still pointing back to choice. The important discipline is that utility is not automatically comparable across people or across arbitrary rescalings. It is a representation chosen for the problem. In expected-utility settings the representation has to carry more structure because lotteries require comparing weighted consequences.
utility.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is that utility preserves the shape of a ranking in a form algebra can manipulate. If higher utility means the player chooses that outcome over another, then best-response calculations can compare numbers instead of verbal preferences. The danger is forgetting which transformations preserve the relevant choice facts.
utility.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating utility points like dollars or happiness units. Sometimes dollars enter utility, but utility itself is the model’s choice index, not necessarily a literal commodity.
utility.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because tables and equations cannot operate directly on vague rankings. Utility turns the ranking into a number while preserving the choice information the model needs. It is the handle that lets the course move from “preferred” to “has the larger payoff in this calculation.”
utility.course_boundary_note: The boundary is scale and interpretation. Utility can support payoff comparison inside the model, but it cannot automatically compare happiness across people or survive arbitrary changes when expected-utility structure is required.

expected_utility.everyday_problem: The problem is choosing when the outcome is uncertain: a bid might win or lose, a risky action might pay off or fail, and a type may be one of several possibilities.
expected_utility.first_principles_reason: This exists because people must act before uncertainty is resolved. A choice must be judged by the whole lottery of possible outcomes, not only by the result that happens afterward.
expected_utility.mathematical_object: The object is expected utility: utility in each possible state weighted by that state's probability. It compresses a risky situation into one comparison number.
expected_utility.operation: Write each possible outcome, attach its probability, multiply probability by utility, and add the pieces.
expected_utility.worked_mini_example: A bidder may win with probability 1/3 and earn 90, or lose with probability 2/3 and earn 0. Expected utility asks whether that gamble beats another bid once all possible results are counted.
expected_utility.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to average dollars automatically. If people care about risk, the utility of money may not rise one-for-one with dollars.
expected_utility.recognize_in_new_work: Look for private information, lotteries, risk, or unknown types where the model has to average payoffs across possible worlds.
expected_utility.why_it_matters: Expected utility matters because strategic choice often happens before uncertainty resolves. A player must compare actions that lead to several possible outcomes, so the course needs a way to combine payoff and likelihood in one decision object.
expected_utility.what_breaks_without_it: Without expected utility, Bayesian games and auctions would have no disciplined way to evaluate actions under unknown types or rival values. The model would either ignore risk or smuggle in an unspecified attitude toward it.
expected_utility.naive_problem: A naive approach picks the most attractive possible outcome and forgets how likely it is. The course instead asks how each possible outcome should count before the player knows which one will arrive.
expected_utility.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a high payoff is extremely unlikely or a modest payoff is nearly certain. Probability changes the choice because the decision is over a lottery, not over a single known result.
expected_utility.lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses expected utility to make uncertainty calculable without removing it. That is why probabilities and utility numbers appear together rather than in separate parts of the model.
expected_utility.cross_course_connections: Expected utility is the arithmetic behind mixed strategies, Bayesian Nash equilibrium, auctions, and belief updating. Whenever the course says a type or action is chosen before hidden information is known, this primitive is working underneath.
expected_utility.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version begins when a player chooses before knowing which outcome will occur. The course cannot use the best or worst possible payoff alone, because the action leads to a lottery. Expected utility says: list the possible outcomes, attach probabilities, translate each outcome into utility, and average. That operation gives the player one comparison number for an uncertain action. Later private-information models use the same move: a bidder or player chooses while averaging over possible types or rival values.
expected_utility.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is weighted bookkeeping. Each possible payoff counts in proportion to how likely that state is. The expectation symbol is not magic; it is the sum of utility in each possible world multiplied by the probability of that world.
expected_utility.student_trap: Students often get stuck by averaging dollar outcomes when the model needs utility outcomes, or by forgetting that the probabilities are beliefs from the player’s point of view rather than facts known after the uncertainty resolves.
expected_utility.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because uncertainty creates bundles of possible outcomes. A player choosing now cannot optimize separately in each future state; they need one comparison for the whole risky action. Expected utility is that comparison, built by weighting each consequence by the probability assigned before the outcome is known.
expected_utility.course_boundary_note: The boundary appears when probabilities or utility over risk are misspecified. Expected utility is a disciplined average, but it does not by itself prove the player has correct beliefs or risk-neutral attitudes.

strategic_form_games.everyday_problem: The problem is representing a situation where everyone chooses without first seeing the others' choices, yet everyone's payoff depends on the whole combination.
strategic_form_games.first_principles_reason: This exists because strategic dependence needs a shared object. A verbal story hides who can choose what and what each combination produces.
strategic_form_games.mathematical_object: The object is a normal-form game: players, action sets, and payoff functions collected into a table or payoff map.
strategic_form_games.operation: Name the players, list each player's available actions, then fill in the payoff for every action profile.
strategic_form_games.worked_mini_example: In prisoner's dilemma, each person chooses confess or stay silent. The payoff in a cell is not caused by one choice alone; it is caused by the pair of choices.
strategic_form_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to read one row or one column as if the other player were irrelevant. The whole point of the table is joint dependence.
strategic_form_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for simultaneous moves, payoff matrices, or models where the exact timing is suppressed so strategic dependence can be seen cleanly.
strategic_form_games.why_it_matters: Strategic form matters because it gives interdependence a minimal representation. By putting each player, action, and payoff in one table, the course can ask dominance, best-response, and Nash questions without losing track of whose choice affects whom.
strategic_form_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without strategic form, simultaneous games would remain verbal scenarios. Students could argue about incentives, but they would lack the structured object needed to compare rows, columns, and deviations cleanly.
strategic_form_games.naive_problem: A naive description tells a story about two players wanting different things. The course needs the sharper object: a list of action combinations and the payoff each player receives at each combination.
strategic_form_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple story fails when a move sounds good alone but earns a different payoff under another player action. Strategic form forces every action to be evaluated inside an action profile.
strategic_form_games.lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses strategic form as the course first serious game representation. The table is not decoration; it is the machine that turns interacting choices into payoffs that can be checked.
strategic_form_games.cross_course_connections: Strategic form supports dominance, iterated deletion, best response, Nash, mixed strategies, and zero-sum analysis. Later trees and Bayesian games are extensions of this representation when timing or hidden information must be shown explicitly.
strategic_form_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version makes the strategic situation flat and inspectable. A strategic-form game lists players, their available actions, and the payoff for each complete action profile. This representation is powerful because it forces the analyst to stop describing one player’s choice alone. Every payoff cell already contains the interaction: my action and your action together. Once the table exists, dominance, best response, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, and zero-sum reasoning can all be asked as precise questions about rows, columns, and cells.
strategic_form_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is a function from action profiles to payoffs. The input is everyone’s action, not one action by itself. The output can be different for each player, which is why the same cell can be attractive to one player and unattractive to another.
strategic_form_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by reading a row as if it has a single value. A row has several consequences, one for each possible opponent action, so a strategy cannot be judged until the contingency is named.
strategic_form_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because strategic dependence needs a container. If each payoff depends on everyone’s action, the model needs a way to list the whole action profile and the payoff consequences together. Strategic form is the simplest object that keeps those dependencies visible and checkable.
strategic_form_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is timing and information. Strategic form is clean for simultaneous or reduced games, but it hides histories and observations unless those are folded into strategies with care.

extensive_form_games.everyday_problem: The problem is that some games unfold over time. A later choice can depend on an earlier choice, and some players may know more about the history than others.
extensive_form_games.first_principles_reason: This exists because timing and information change incentives. A threat that sounds good at the start may not be attractive when the threatened moment arrives.
extensive_form_games.mathematical_object: The object is a game tree: decision nodes, branches, histories, information sets, and terminal payoffs.
extensive_form_games.operation: Draw the order of moves, show what each player knows at each decision point, then reason from the end or through beliefs depending on the information structure.
extensive_form_games.worked_mini_example: In an entry game, an incumbent may threaten a price war after entry. The tree asks whether fighting is actually optimal once entry has happened.
extensive_form_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to collapse every sequential game into a payoff matrix and lose the credibility problem.
extensive_form_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for histories, decision nodes, information sets, or any claim where the order of moves changes what behavior can be believed.
extensive_form_games.why_it_matters: Extensive form matters because timing can change strategy. A player who moves later may observe history, respond to threats, or condition action on earlier choices, and those possibilities cannot be represented honestly in a flat simultaneous table.
extensive_form_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without extensive form, the course could mistake a sequential conflict for a simultaneous one. That would hide credibility, information sets, and the fact that later choices can make earlier announcements meaningful or empty.
extensive_form_games.naive_problem: A naive approach lists each person choices and ignores when they are made. The course asks whether a player moves before or after seeing another action, because that timing can change the entire prediction.
extensive_form_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a threat or promise is evaluated as if it were binding from the start. In a tree, the later decision node asks whether the threat would still be chosen after the history occurs.
extensive_form_games.lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses game trees to make histories visible. Nodes, branches, and information sets are teaching devices for asking what each player knows and can choose at each point.
extensive_form_games.cross_course_connections: Extensive form connects directly to backward induction, subgame perfection, bargaining, one-shot deviation, and PBE. It is the representation that lets credibility and belief updating become mathematical rather than rhetorical.
extensive_form_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version asks what the table hides. If players move in sequence, observe earlier actions, or choose after reaching different histories, the game needs a tree. The tree records decision nodes, branches, histories, payoffs at terminal nodes, and information sets when a player cannot distinguish where they are. This representation is not visual decoration. It is what lets the course ask whether a threat is credible, whether a later player observes an earlier choice, and whether beliefs must be updated after a signal.
extensive_form_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is recursive structure. A node summarizes a history, an action selects a branch, and a terminal path gives payoffs. The tree turns time into an object that backward induction and subgame perfection can operate on.
extensive_form_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by assuming a tree automatically means everyone observed every earlier move. Information sets matter because the same physical history and the same known history are not always the same thing.
extensive_form_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because time and information change what an action means. A flat list of actions cannot say who moved first, what was observed, or which histories a player can distinguish. The tree structure preserves those facts so later credibility and belief questions have a place to attach.
extensive_form_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is representational honesty. A tree can only support credible conclusions if its nodes, information sets, and payoffs capture what players actually know and can choose.

dominance.everyday_problem: The problem is that some choices are plainly bad no matter what the other side does. Keeping them in the analysis can distract from the strategic choices that actually need thought.
dominance.first_principles_reason: Dominance exists because comparison can sometimes be made without beliefs. If one action beats another across every possible opponent action, the worse action does not need a prediction about opponents to be rejected.
dominance.mathematical_object: The object is a dominance comparison between two strategies across all possible actions by others.
dominance.operation: Compare one strategy to another row by row or column by column. If it is never worse and sometimes better, it dominates; if it is always strictly better, it strictly dominates.
dominance.worked_mini_example: If a firm earns less from pricing high than pricing low no matter what the rival does, high pricing is dominated in that model. The firm does not need to forecast the rival before rejecting it.
dominance.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to delete a strategy because it feels unlikely. Dominance is a universal comparison, not a hunch.
dominance.recognize_in_new_work: Look for arguments that rule out actions before equilibrium is computed because one action is never a best answer.
dominance.why_it_matters: Dominance matters because it is one of the cleanest places where rationality has bite without requiring a forecast. If an action loses to another action in every relevant contingency, the course can reject it before solving the full strategic puzzle.
dominance.what_breaks_without_it: Without dominance, every listed strategy would look equally alive even when some choices have no defensible reason to be played. The analysis would be noisier and less disciplined before equilibrium reasoning even begins.
dominance.naive_problem: A naive approach deletes a move because it looks unlikely or unpopular. The dominance test is stricter: it asks whether another move does at least as well against every opponent action and better somewhere.
dominance.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a strategy is bad under one opponent action but useful under another. That is not dominance; that is a belief-dependent tradeoff that must be handled by best response or rationalizability.
dominance.lecture_emphasis: The dominance lecture teaches pruning as a mathematical comparison, not as taste. The important move is checking all opponent actions before saying a strategy is never worth keeping.
dominance.cross_course_connections: Dominance leads into iterated deletion and rationalizability, and it also prepares the ground for Nash because dominated strategies cannot be serious best responses. Its limit explains why beliefs later become necessary.
dominance.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version shows a rare moment where beliefs are unnecessary. To test dominance, compare one strategy with another against every possible opponent action. If one strategy is never worse and sometimes better, the inferior strategy has no reason to survive. The key is the universal quantifier: every contingency must be checked. This is why dominance is strong but limited. It can clean up a game before equilibrium reasoning, but many strategies are not dominated even though they may fail later tests.
dominance.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is an inequality repeated across columns, states, or opponent actions. The concept says the comparison does not depend on a forecast. If the inequality holds everywhere, no belief about the opponent can rescue the dominated strategy.
dominance.student_trap: Students often get stuck by deleting strategies that are merely unattractive under their favorite prediction. That is not dominance. A strategy that is bad against one opponent move but useful against another is belief-dependent, not dominated.
dominance.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because some choices can be rejected without forecasting the opponent. The dominance comparison formalizes “no matter what they do” as a set of inequalities across contingencies. That makes deletion a proof about payoffs rather than a guess about likely behavior.
dominance.course_boundary_note: The boundary is strength. Dominance is decisive when it applies, but many live strategies are not dominated. Those cases need beliefs, best responses, or equilibrium instead of more aggressive deletion.

iterated_deletion.everyday_problem: The problem is that once obviously bad moves are removed, new moves may become obviously bad in the smaller game.
iterated_deletion.first_principles_reason: This exists because reasoning about rational players is recursive. I can remove my dominated action, then you can reason that I removed it, then your own comparison may change.
iterated_deletion.mathematical_object: The object is a reduced game created by repeated dominance pruning.
iterated_deletion.operation: Delete dominated strategies, rebuild the smaller strategic environment, and repeat until no more deletions are justified under the chosen dominance rule.
iterated_deletion.worked_mini_example: In a guessing game, very high guesses may be impossible for a rational winner; once those are removed, the next-highest guesses become impossible too. The deletion process walks inward.
iterated_deletion.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to ignore whether the deletion uses strict or weak dominance. Weak deletion can depend on order and needs more care.
iterated_deletion.recognize_in_new_work: Look for step-by-step elimination arguments where rationality of others is used more than once.
iterated_deletion.why_it_matters: Iterated deletion matters because strategic reasoning can be recursive. Removing one unreasonable choice can make another choice unreasonable in the smaller game, so rationality can propagate through the table in stages.
iterated_deletion.what_breaks_without_it: Without iterated deletion, the course would miss how one round of reasoning changes the next. Some games reveal their strategic structure only after obviously dominated actions are removed and the remaining incentives are reconsidered.
iterated_deletion.naive_problem: A naive approach performs one deletion pass and stops. The course asks what the remaining players know after the first pass and whether the reduced game creates new dominance comparisons.
iterated_deletion.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when students treat deletion as bookkeeping rather than reasoning about shared rationality. Each round means players understand that earlier bad moves have been ruled out.
iterated_deletion.lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses deletion to show that rationality assumptions can have layers. The operation is mechanical, but the interpretation is about what players can infer from others being rational too.
iterated_deletion.cross_course_connections: Iterated deletion connects dominance to rationalizability and common knowledge. It also contrasts with Nash: deletion rules can narrow the game before equilibrium, but they do not always select a single stable prediction.
iterated_deletion.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version adds recursion to dominance. After dominated strategies are removed, the remaining game is no longer the same game for reasoning purposes. A strategy that was not dominated before can become dominated after the opponent’s unreasonable options disappear. This creates a chain of inference: I rule out your dominated move, you rule out mine, and so on. The operation is simple, but its interpretation is deep because it depends on players understanding rationality and sometimes understanding that others understand it.
iterated_deletion.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is repeated pruning over a shrinking action set. Each round applies the dominance comparison to the reduced game, so the domain of possible opponent actions changes as the procedure proceeds.
iterated_deletion.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating the order of deletion and the type of dominance as harmless details. With weak dominance especially, those details can change what remains, so the lecture distinction matters.
iterated_deletion.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because rationality can be layered. Once one impossible action is removed, the remaining problem changes, and new impossibilities can appear. Iterated deletion is the formal procedure that keeps track of that changing action set instead of relying on informal rounds of intuition.
iterated_deletion.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the deletion rule. Strict deletion has a different force than weak deletion, and common knowledge assumptions matter when interpreting many rounds of pruning. The boundary is why the lecture distinguishes the procedure from equilibrium selection. Surviving deletion means a strategy has not been ruled out by that rationality test; it does not mean the strategy will be played.

rationalizability.everyday_problem: The problem is deciding which strategies can be defended as sensible without requiring everyone to land on one exact equilibrium.
rationalizability.first_principles_reason: This exists because a strategy can be rational under some belief even if it is not part of the final equilibrium prediction. The course needs a wider plausibility test than Nash equilibrium.
rationalizability.mathematical_object: The object is a set of strategies that survive because each can be a best response to some belief about the other players' surviving strategies.
rationalizability.operation: Ask whether there exists a belief under which the strategy is optimal. If no such belief exists, the strategy cannot be rationalized.
rationalizability.worked_mini_example: Suppose a player chooses an action that is not your favorite prediction. The rationalizability question is not whether you expected it. It is whether some coherent belief about the opponent could make that action best. If the action pays well when the opponent is likely to choose left, and the player could reasonably believe left is likely, the action survives. If no probability over the opponent actions can make it best, the action is not rationalizable.
rationalizability.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat rationalizable as meaning correct or predicted. It means defensible under some belief, not uniquely expected.
rationalizability.recognize_in_new_work: Look for models that want to separate impossible behavior from behavior that is merely one of several plausible responses.
rationalizability.why_it_matters: Rationalizability matters because not every plausible strategy must belong to a Nash equilibrium. The course needs a way to ask whether a move could be optimal under some coherent belief about others.
rationalizability.what_breaks_without_it: Without rationalizability, students may jump too quickly from dominance to Nash. They would miss the middle ground where a strategy survives because a player can hold a belief that makes it a best response.
rationalizability.naive_problem: A naive approach says a surprising move is irrational because it is not what the analyst expected. Rationalizability asks a better question: is there any belief about others that would make the move optimal?
rationalizability.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the modeler treats their own forecast as the only possible belief. Game theory often needs to distinguish unreasonable actions from reasonable actions under different expectations.
rationalizability.lecture_emphasis: The rationalizability lecture shifts attention from deleting impossible moves to supporting possible ones. Beliefs become the object that explains why a surviving strategy can make sense.
rationalizability.cross_course_connections: Rationalizability shares the best-response primitive with Nash but relaxes mutual consistency. It also previews Bayesian thinking because beliefs become explicit inputs to choice rather than background intuition.
rationalizability.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version sits between dominance and Nash equilibrium. Dominance asks whether an action is never worth taking. Nash asks whether everyone actions and beliefs fit together in one mutually consistent profile. Rationalizability occupies the middle: keep a strategy if it can be optimal for some belief about what other players choose. That is why the lecture begins by recalling what a belief is. The belief is not decorative psychology; it is the support structure that can hold a strategy up. The best-response requirement still disciplines the idea, because the belief must make the action optimal rather than merely imaginable.
rationalizability.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is support by belief. Instead of asking whether strategies match each other exactly, ask whether there exists a probability distribution over others’ actions that makes the strategy maximize expected payoff.
rationalizability.student_trap: Students often get stuck because rationalizability feels permissive. It is permissive on purpose, but not empty: a strategy still has to be a best response to some belief, not just a move someone might randomly choose.
rationalizability.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because plausibility is belief-dependent. A move can look strange from the outside and still be rational for someone who expects different opponent behavior. Ordinary language cannot keep those cases straight: it tends to collapse surprising, wrong, irrational, and non-equilibrium into one bucket. Rationalizability separates them. The math asks whether there exists a probability distribution over the other players surviving strategies such that this action maximizes expected payoff. Existence is the key word: the belief need not be the analyst final forecast, but it must be coherent enough to make the action a best response.
rationalizability.course_boundary_note: The boundary is mutual consistency. Rationalizability can defend a strategy from one player perspective, but it does not prove that all players beliefs are correct together. A rationalizable strategy may survive because one belief supports it, while Nash requires each player strategy to be a best response to the strategies others actually use in the proposed profile. That is why rationalizability is useful but deliberately weaker than equilibrium.

best_response.everyday_problem: The problem is that a strategy is not good in the abstract. It is good against a particular opponent action or belief.
best_response.first_principles_reason: This exists because strategic choice is conditional. The same move can be excellent against one opponent move and terrible against another.
best_response.mathematical_object: The object is the best-response set: all actions that maximize a player's payoff given the other side's action or belief.
best_response.operation: Fix what the player thinks others will do, compare the player's own available actions, and keep the payoff-maximizing action or actions.
best_response.worked_mini_example: If a store believes its rival will keep prices high, matching high prices may be best; if the rival cuts prices, cutting may become best. The best response changes with the condition.
best_response.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to ask whether an action is rational without saying against what belief.
best_response.recognize_in_new_work: Look for arrows, reaction functions, or optimization steps that start with given the other player does X.
best_response.why_it_matters: Best response matters because it is the local engine of strategic reasoning. Before any equilibrium concept is introduced, the course needs the conditional question: if the environment is fixed this way, which action gives this player the highest payoff?
best_response.what_breaks_without_it: Without best response, equilibrium would be a name without a test. The course could not check Nash profiles, bidding functions, mixed strategies, or type-contingent plans because each requires a player-level optimality calculation.
best_response.naive_problem: A naive approach asks whether an action is rational in the abstract. The course insists on the missing phrase: rational given what belief, opponent action, information set, or continuation value?
best_response.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the same action changes status across contingencies. Cutting price, bidding high, or sending a message can be best in one environment and poor in another.
best_response.lecture_emphasis: The best-response lecture teaches conditional optimization in plain strategic form. It is the small repeated operation that later hides inside reaction curves, equilibrium checks, and auction bidding equations.
best_response.cross_course_connections: Best response connects to Nash, mixed strategies, minimax, Bayesian Nash, PBE, and mechanism design. Each later solution concept changes what is held fixed, but the conditional choice question remains.
best_response.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version is the small engine that powers the rest of the course. A best response is not a universally good action; it is the action that performs best once another action, belief, type, or history is held fixed. This is why the phrase “given” matters. Given the rival price, choose a price. Given the opponent mixture, choose a pure action or mix. Given beliefs about types, choose the highest expected payoff. Every equilibrium concept repeats this local test under a broader consistency requirement.
best_response.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is argmax: search over the player’s available actions and keep the action or actions with the largest payoff under the specified condition. The condition is part of the object, not background prose.
best_response.student_trap: Students often get stuck by saying an action is rational without saying relative to what. The missing belief or opponent action is usually where the real assumption is hiding.
best_response.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because “good strategy” is incomplete without a condition. The best-response set stores the actions that maximize payoff given a named opponent action or belief. It is the reusable local object behind equilibrium, auctions, and dynamic deviation checks.
best_response.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the condition being held fixed. A best response tells the right action only after the opponent action, belief, type, or history has been named. This is why every later equilibrium check starts locally before making a global claim.

nash_equilibrium.everyday_problem: The problem is making a prediction that does not immediately fall apart when each participant asks, given what the others are doing, should I switch?
nash_equilibrium.first_principles_reason: Nash equilibrium exists because a strategic prediction has to be self-consistent. If one player wants to change after seeing the proposed profile, the profile was not a stable prediction.
nash_equilibrium.mathematical_object: The object is an action or strategy profile where every player's choice is a best response to the others' choices.
nash_equilibrium.operation: Check each player one at a time. Hold the other players fixed and ask whether that player can improve by changing alone. If nobody can, the profile is Nash.
nash_equilibrium.worked_mini_example: At a four-way stop, everyone going at once is not stable if each driver would rather wait or avoid collision given the others. A stable traffic convention must make each driver's move sensible given the convention.
nash_equilibrium.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to hear equilibrium and think socially best. Nash can describe bad outcomes, including prisoner's dilemma, because it is about unilateral incentives, not collective welfare.
nash_equilibrium.recognize_in_new_work: Look for claims that a behavior pattern persists because no individual participant can gain by deviating alone.
nash_equilibrium.why_it_matters: Nash matters because it gives the course a baseline standard for strategic stability. It does not promise that the outcome is good; it says the proposed behavior survives each player privately checking whether a one-person switch would pay.
nash_equilibrium.what_breaks_without_it: Without Nash equilibrium, payoff tables would produce stories but not disciplined predictions. Any outcome could be proposed even if one participant has an obvious profitable deviation once everyone else behavior is named.
nash_equilibrium.naive_problem: A naive approach calls an observed pattern an outcome and moves on. Nash asks whether that pattern can hold together after every player asks, given the others, would I rather change?
nash_equilibrium.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the analyst checks only total payoff or social appeal. A collectively attractive outcome can still fail if one player can improve by deviating alone.
nash_equilibrium.lecture_emphasis: The Nash lecture is the course central stability lesson. The key move is not the word equilibrium; it is the repeated deviation audit, player by player, against the proposed profile.
nash_equilibrium.cross_course_connections: Nash connects backward to best response and forward to mixed strategies, subgame perfection, Bayesian Nash, and PBE. Each refinement keeps the same no-profitable-deviation core while repairing a missing feature such as time or private information.
nash_equilibrium.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version takes best response and closes the loop. A Nash equilibrium is a whole profile where every player’s action passes the best-response test against the others. It is a fixed point of strategic expectations: each person’s plan makes sense because the others’ plans are what they are. The course uses this to discipline prediction. A proposed outcome cannot merely sound plausible or efficient; it must survive each participant’s unilateral deviation check.
nash_equilibrium.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is mutual best response. For every player i, the chosen action a_i must sit inside BR_i(a_-i). The notation says no one can improve by changing only their own component while the rest of the profile is held still.
nash_equilibrium.student_trap: Students often get stuck by importing the everyday meaning of equilibrium as balance or goodness. Nash equilibrium can be inefficient or ugly. Its claim is narrower: no single player wants to move alone.
nash_equilibrium.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because strategic prediction is circular. Each player’s best action depends on the others’ actions, so the model needs a profile where all those conditional choices fit together. Nash equilibrium is the formal closure of the best-response loop.
nash_equilibrium.course_boundary_note: The boundary is one-person deviation from a fixed profile. Nash does not handle noncredible threats, belief updating, coalitional deviations, or welfare without extra structure.

mixed_strategies.everyday_problem: The problem is what to predict when choosing one pure action would make a player exploitable or when no pure-action equilibrium exists.
mixed_strategies.first_principles_reason: Mixed strategies exist because unpredictability can itself be strategic. Randomizing can make the opponent indifferent, preventing them from targeting a predictable move.
mixed_strategies.mathematical_object: The object is a probability distribution over pure strategies, often chosen so the other player has no strict favorite response.
mixed_strategies.operation: Assign probabilities to actions, compute the opponent's expected payoff from each response, and choose probabilities that make the opponent willing to mix or unable to exploit you.
mixed_strategies.worked_mini_example: In penalty kicks, always shooting left invites the goalie to dive left. Mixing left and right makes the goalie's guessing problem hard enough that neither side has a simple pure advantage.
mixed_strategies.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to think mixed strategy means confusion. In the model, randomization can be deliberate and exactly calculated.
mixed_strategies.recognize_in_new_work: Look for indifference equations, randomized play, or models where predictable behavior would be punished.
mixed_strategies.why_it_matters: Mixed strategies matter because predictability can be strategically costly. When no fixed action can be stable, deliberate randomization can make opponents indifferent enough that the overall behavior survives best-response checks.
mixed_strategies.what_breaks_without_it: Without mixed strategies, the course would falsely conclude that some games have no stable prediction simply because no pure action profile works. It would also miss why randomness can be chosen as discipline rather than noise.
mixed_strategies.naive_problem: A naive approach treats random play as confusion or lack of strategy. The course reframes it as a planned probability distribution that changes what opponents can exploit.
mixed_strategies.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails in games like matching pennies, where any predictable pure move gives the opponent a profitable response. Stability requires making the opponent unable to improve by targeting a pattern.
mixed_strategies.lecture_emphasis: The mixed-strategy lecture teaches students to solve for probabilities that make another player willing to mix. Indifference is not a side detail; it is the mathematical condition that pins down the mixture.
mixed_strategies.cross_course_connections: Mixed strategies connect Nash to zero-sum games, minimax, and expected utility. The player is not choosing one payoff; they are choosing a distribution whose expected consequences shape the opponent response.
mixed_strategies.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version explains why randomization can be chosen deliberately. In some games, every predictable action can be exploited. A mixed strategy turns choice into a probability distribution over actions, and the equilibrium mixture often makes the opponent indifferent among the actions they are willing to use. The randomness is therefore strategic. It changes the opponent’s payoff comparison, which changes what can be stable.
mixed_strategies.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is expected payoff under probabilities. If the opponent mixes, each of my pure actions has an expected payoff. In equilibrium, actions used with positive probability must usually earn the same expected payoff, otherwise I would shift probability toward the better one.
mixed_strategies.student_trap: Students often get stuck by asking what the player “really” chooses. The answer is that the random device is part of the strategy; after it realizes an action, the distribution was still the planned commitment.
mixed_strategies.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because pure actions cannot always carry stable predictions. A probability distribution over actions lets the player control predictability itself. The distribution becomes the strategy because it determines opponents’ expected payoffs before the random action is realized.
mixed_strategies.course_boundary_note: The boundary is interpretation and commitment. A mixed strategy is useful when randomization is credible and payoff-relevant, but not every observed frequency is an equilibrium mixture. The boundary is that the model predicts a distribution, not necessarily a visible sequence that looks random in a small sample. Interpreting observed play requires care about commitment, learning, and repeated sampling.

zero_sum_games.everyday_problem: The problem is pure conflict: one side's gain is the other side's loss, so cooperation or joint surplus is not the issue.
zero_sum_games.first_principles_reason: This exists because some strategic settings are distributional rather than productive. The total pie is fixed; strategy determines who gets it.
zero_sum_games.mathematical_object: The object is a payoff function where player two's payoff is the negative of player one's payoff.
zero_sum_games.operation: Represent the game from one player's payoff table, because the other player's payoff moves in the opposite direction. Then search for secure strategies and equilibrium value.
zero_sum_games.worked_mini_example: In matching pennies, if one player wins a dollar the other loses a dollar. There is no both-win cell; the only question is how each side avoids being exploited.
zero_sum_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to apply zero-sum intuition to bargaining or market games where joint gains are possible.
zero_sum_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for adversarial models where maximizing my payoff is exactly minimizing yours.
zero_sum_games.why_it_matters: Zero-sum games matter because they isolate pure conflict. When one player gain is exactly the other loss, equilibrium reasoning becomes a question of value, protection, and exploitability.
zero_sum_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without the zero-sum distinction, students may apply adversarial security logic to games where cooperation or joint surplus exists. The course needs this special case precisely because its conclusions are sharper than in general games.
zero_sum_games.naive_problem: A naive approach treats every competitive setting as zero-sum. The course asks whether payoffs really move in exact opposition or whether there are gains, losses, or inefficiencies shared by both sides.
zero_sum_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when rivalry coexists with mutual gains from agreement. Pricing, bargaining, and auctions can be competitive without being literally zero-sum.
zero_sum_games.lecture_emphasis: The zero-sum lecture clarifies the environment where security-level reasoning is most justified. The payoff structure, not the intensity of conflict, determines whether the zero-sum tools apply.
zero_sum_games.cross_course_connections: Zero-sum games connect mixed strategies to minimax. They also mark a boundary with bargaining, repeated cooperation, and mechanism design, where the central issue is not only defeating the other side.
zero_sum_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version isolates exact opposition. In a zero-sum game, one player’s payoff can be treated as the negative of the other’s payoff, so the entire conflict has a single value from opposite perspectives. This lets the course make stronger claims than in general games. Security, value, saddle points, and minimax reasoning become central because there is no hidden joint surplus to unlock through cooperation.
zero_sum_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is payoff conservation. If player 1 gets u, player 2 gets -u. That structure means maximizing one side’s payoff is equivalent to minimizing the other side’s payoff, which is why max and min operations meet.
zero_sum_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by calling any rivalry zero-sum. Many competitive economic settings still have joint gains, inefficiencies, or possibilities for collusion. Zero-sum is a payoff structure, not a mood.
zero_sum_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because exact conflict has special structure. When one player’s payoff is the negative of the other’s, the model can collapse two objectives into one value seen from opposite sides. That structure justifies security and minimax tools that would be too strong in general games.
zero_sum_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is exact payoff opposition. If players can both gain, both lose, bargain, collude, or create surplus, zero-sum tools can distort the strategic picture. The boundary helps students avoid overusing adversarial language. A market competitor can hurt you and still not be in a zero-sum game if pricing, entry, innovation, or collusion changes total surplus.

minimax.everyday_problem: The problem is choosing under hostile response: what can I guarantee if the other side tries to hurt me as much as possible?
minimax.first_principles_reason: Minimax exists because in zero-sum conflict, optimism is dangerous. The opponent is not nature; the opponent is choosing against you.
minimax.mathematical_object: The object is a security calculation: maximize the minimum payoff you can be forced to accept, or minimize the maximum damage the opponent can impose.
minimax.operation: For each strategy, look at the worst payoff it could lead to. Then choose the strategy with the best worst-case number.
minimax.worked_mini_example: A chess player does not evaluate a move by assuming the opponent will blunder. Minimax-style reasoning asks what survives the opponent's strongest reply.
minimax.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to use minimax as a general decision rule in games that are not zero-sum or not adversarial in that strict way.
minimax.recognize_in_new_work: Look for worst-case guarantees, security levels, or saddle-point reasoning.
minimax.why_it_matters: Minimax matters because it formalizes defensive reasoning. In adversarial settings, a player may want a strategy whose worst possible consequence is as good as it can be, even before knowing exactly how the opponent will attack.
minimax.what_breaks_without_it: Without minimax, the course could describe conflict but not the logic of protecting against exploitation. It would miss why randomization and worst-case evaluation can produce a stable value in zero-sum games.
minimax.naive_problem: A naive approach chooses the action with the best-looking upside. Minimax asks what happens if the opponent sees the plan and chooses the response that hurts most.
minimax.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the high-upside action has a terrible weakness. In a hostile setting, the opponent is not sampling randomly from your hopes; they are choosing against you.
minimax.lecture_emphasis: The minimax lecture teaches students to read a payoff table through security levels. The important calculation is not average attractiveness but the guarantee preserved under the opponent best attack.
minimax.cross_course_connections: Minimax connects to zero-sum value, mixed strategies, and best response. It also foreshadows robustness ideas outside game theory, but the course version is grounded in exact payoff opposition.
minimax.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version teaches adversarial caution. Instead of asking which action has the best upside, minimax asks which strategy has the best guarantee against the opponent’s most damaging response. This is natural in zero-sum games because the opponent wants exactly what hurts you. The course uses minimax to show how mixed strategies can protect a player by preventing the opponent from exploiting a predictable weakness.
minimax.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is nested comparison. For each strategy, compute the worst payoff the opponent can force. Then choose the strategy whose worst case is largest. In zero-sum equilibrium, this security level lines up with the game’s value.
minimax.student_trap: Students often get stuck by confusing minimax with pessimism. It is not a personality trait; it is the rational response to a modeled opponent whose payoff is opposed to yours.
minimax.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because adversarial choice requires a guarantee. The player needs to compare strategies by what the opponent can force against them. Minimax turns that defensive question into a nested optimization: protect the worst case, then choose the best protection.
minimax.course_boundary_note: The boundary is adversarial structure. Minimax is appropriate when the opponent is modeled as choosing to hurt your payoff; it can be too conservative in cooperative or incomplete-information settings. The boundary also explains why minimax is attractive in some technical fields but not a universal behavioral theory. It gives a guarantee under hostile response; it does not describe trust, learning, bargaining, or mutually beneficial adjustment.

backward_induction.everyday_problem: The problem is that early choices in a tree depend on what later players will actually do, not what they announce they might do.
backward_induction.first_principles_reason: Backward induction exists because the future constrains the present. If we can solve the last decision first, that answer becomes an input into the previous decision.
backward_induction.mathematical_object: The object is a game tree with continuation values assigned from the terminal nodes backward.
backward_induction.operation: Start at the final decision nodes, choose the best branch for the player moving there, replace that subgame with its value, and continue backward to the start.
backward_induction.worked_mini_example: If a parent threatens a punishment they will not want to impose later, a child may ignore it. Backward induction exposes that by checking the later choice first.
backward_induction.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to reason from the start while treating later threats as fixed facts.
backward_induction.recognize_in_new_work: Look for finite sequential games where the last move can be solved and folded back into earlier choices.
backward_induction.why_it_matters: Backward induction matters because sequential rationality starts at the end. The course uses it to show that earlier decisions already contain beliefs about later incentives, so solving forward without checking the end can validate empty threats.
backward_induction.what_breaks_without_it: Without backward induction, a game tree would be a picture of possible histories but not a method for evaluating them. The model could accept plans that later players would abandon once their decision node is reached.
backward_induction.naive_problem: A naive approach begins at the root and follows the most dramatic story. Backward induction begins at the last decision because that is where strategic uncertainty about future incentives is easiest to remove.
backward_induction.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a current action depends on a future threat. If the future threat is not optimal later, it should not influence the earlier player in the predicted way.
backward_induction.lecture_emphasis: The backward-induction lecture turns credibility into an algorithm. By replacing solved terminal pieces with continuation values, it teaches that time can be reasoned through recursively.
backward_induction.cross_course_connections: Backward induction connects extensive form to subgame perfection, bargaining, finite repetition, and one-shot deviation. It is the recursion primitive behind the course treatment of time.
backward_induction.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version begins at the end because the end is where future speculation stops. At a final decision node, the moving player simply chooses the best available branch. Once that branch is known, the earlier node can treat the solved continuation as a value. Repeating that step back to the root gives a path through the tree. The method teaches that an early action is rational only after the later consequences it anticipates are themselves rational.
backward_induction.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is recursion over continuation values. A node’s value is determined by the best value available at the next nodes for the player moving there. The game is solved by replacing future subtrees with their strategic value.
backward_induction.student_trap: Students often get stuck by reading the tree chronologically. Players live forward, but the analyst solves backward because later incentives determine which earlier expectations are credible.
backward_induction.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because sequential choice has nested future problems inside current decisions. A continuation value lets the solved future replace a whole subtree. Without that object, the analyst would have to carry every possible future story instead of using the later incentive calculation.
backward_induction.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the tree. Backward induction is only as good as the modeled histories, payoffs, and information. Hidden information or imperfect observation requires richer tools. The boundary becomes visible when real players have limited foresight or when the tree is not common knowledge. The course model assumes the relevant future choices are understood well enough to be folded backward.

subgame_perfection.everyday_problem: The problem is that Nash equilibrium can allow plans based on threats that would not be carried out if the threatened moment arrived.
subgame_perfection.first_principles_reason: Subgame perfection exists because a strategy should be credible after every history, not only from the starting point.
subgame_perfection.mathematical_object: The object is a Nash equilibrium that also induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
subgame_perfection.operation: Find every proper subgame, solve behavior there, and reject strategy profiles whose continuation play stops being optimal after some history.
subgame_perfection.worked_mini_example: An incumbent firm may threaten to fight entry, but if fighting loses money after entry occurs, the threat is not subgame perfect. The entrant should not be convinced by it.
subgame_perfection.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to think any Nash equilibrium in a dynamic game is credible.
subgame_perfection.recognize_in_new_work: Look for dynamic games, off-path histories, or threats where the key question is whether the promised future action would really be optimal.
subgame_perfection.why_it_matters: Subgame perfection matters because it repairs Nash equilibrium for dynamic games. It asks whether the equilibrium behavior remains rational after every history where the continuation game can be considered on its own.
subgame_perfection.what_breaks_without_it: Without subgame perfection, dynamic models can rest on noncredible threats. A strategy profile may pass the initial Nash test only because it prescribes off-path behavior that nobody would actually choose later.
subgame_perfection.naive_problem: A naive approach checks equilibrium only from the start. The course asks a harsher question: if the game reaches a later subgame, does the prescribed continuation still make strategic sense?
subgame_perfection.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails in entry-deterrence and bargaining-style examples where a player threatens costly punishment. If punishment is irrational after entry, the threat cannot discipline entry before it happens.
subgame_perfection.lecture_emphasis: The subgame-perfection lecture shows why off-path plans are part of credibility. The solution concept is not extra vocabulary; it is the course answer to Nash equilibria that survive only by hiding bad continuation play.
subgame_perfection.cross_course_connections: Subgame perfection connects Nash to backward induction and one-shot deviation. PBE later extends the same credibility demand when hidden information means beliefs must be specified too.
subgame_perfection.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version asks Nash equilibrium to pass inside the tree, not only at the root. A dynamic-game strategy describes what players would do after histories that may never happen on the predicted path. Those off-path prescriptions matter because they can support or undermine threats. Subgame perfection rejects equilibria whose continuation play would fail the Nash test in a proper subgame.
subgame_perfection.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is equilibrium at every credible starting point. A subgame is a piece of the original tree that can be considered as a game on its own. The strategy profile must induce Nash behavior in each such piece.
subgame_perfection.student_trap: Students often get stuck by ignoring histories that do not occur in equilibrium. Those histories are exactly where empty threats hide, so the course makes students inspect them.
subgame_perfection.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because a dynamic strategy includes plans for histories that may not occur. Those plans can support threats, so they must be checked. Subgame perfection formalizes the demand that continuation behavior is itself equilibrium behavior wherever a real subgame begins.
subgame_perfection.course_boundary_note: The boundary is subgames. Some dynamic information problems do not have proper subgames at the histories where beliefs matter, which is why PBE enters later. This boundary is why the course later needs belief-based refinements. Some histories are inside clean subgames, but hidden-information histories can require the analyst to specify what players believe before optimal continuation play can even be evaluated. The refinement is small in wording but large in what behavior it rules out.

one_shot_deviation.everyday_problem: The problem is checking a whole dynamic strategy can be exhausting because a strategy describes what to do after many histories.
one_shot_deviation.first_principles_reason: The one-shot deviation principle exists because, in the right finite or discounted settings, profitable complex deviations reveal themselves through a profitable single-period deviation.
one_shot_deviation.mathematical_object: The object is a local deviation test: change one action at one history while leaving the continuation strategy fixed.
one_shot_deviation.operation: Hold the proposed strategy fixed everywhere except one decision point. If no one can gain from any one-shot change, the strategy passes the shortcut test under the theorem's assumptions.
one_shot_deviation.worked_mini_example: Instead of checking every possible plan for a repeated-game player, check whether cheating today and returning to the plan tomorrow pays. If even that one-step cheat fails everywhere, the larger plan may be safe.
one_shot_deviation.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to use the shortcut without checking the assumptions that make local deviations enough.
one_shot_deviation.recognize_in_new_work: Look for dynamic incentive proofs that replace many possible deviations with a one-period deviation inequality.
one_shot_deviation.why_it_matters: The one-shot deviation principle matters because dynamic strategies can contain many possible deviations. The principle gives a manageable local test when its conditions hold: if no single-period change helps, longer deviations need not be separately checked.
one_shot_deviation.what_breaks_without_it: Without this principle, verifying repeated or dynamic equilibria can become intractable. Students may either skip deviation checks or drown in too many possible alternative histories.
one_shot_deviation.naive_problem: A naive approach tries to compare a proposed strategy with every imaginable replacement strategy at once. The course introduces a sharper local question: can the player gain by changing just one action at one history?
one_shot_deviation.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a long deviation looks mysterious but is really built from local profitable steps. The principle works only under the right dynamic conditions, so the shortcut itself has assumptions.
one_shot_deviation.lecture_emphasis: The lecture emphasizes the principle as a verification tool, not a new behavioral assumption. It helps students audit dynamic optimality without losing sight of the incentive logic.
one_shot_deviation.cross_course_connections: One-shot deviation connects subgame perfection to repeated games and trigger strategies. It uses the same credibility primitive as backward induction but applies it to richer strategy plans.
one_shot_deviation.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version solves a verification problem. Dynamic strategies are long objects: they say what to do after many histories. Checking every possible alternative strategy can be impossible by hand. Under the principle’s conditions, it is enough to check whether a player can gain by changing one action at one history while otherwise returning to the proposed strategy. That local test can certify the larger plan.
one_shot_deviation.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is local optimality implying global optimality in the relevant dynamic environment. If no single stitch can be profitably pulled out, then a longer deviation cannot be assembled profitably from such local changes.
one_shot_deviation.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating the principle as universally available. It depends on the structure of the dynamic game, so the shortcut must travel with its assumptions.
one_shot_deviation.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because dynamic strategies are too large to compare naively. A local deviation test gives the course a finite, teachable way to verify optimality under the right assumptions. It turns the huge space of possible strategy changes into a sequence of one-history checks.
one_shot_deviation.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the theorem conditions. The shortcut cannot be used blindly in every dynamic game; the structure must justify local checks standing in for global deviations. The boundary is also pedagogical: the principle is a theorem that saves work, not a license to ignore dynamic incentives. Students still need to know what histories and one-step deviations must be checked.

bargaining.everyday_problem: The problem is dividing gains from agreement when each side would like more of the surplus and can sometimes wait, reject, or walk away.
bargaining.first_principles_reason: Bargaining exists because conflict and cooperation are intertwined. There is value to agreement, but disagreement over division changes each side's threat point.
bargaining.mathematical_object: The object is a bargaining game with offers, acceptance rules, disagreement payoffs, and sometimes discounting.
bargaining.operation: Identify the surplus, each side's outside option, who makes offers, and how delay changes payoffs; then solve for which offers can be accepted.
bargaining.worked_mini_example: If a seller values a car at 8,000 and a buyer values it at 10,000, trade creates 2,000 of surplus. Bargaining asks who captures that surplus and why.
bargaining.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat bargaining power as a vague personality trait when the model usually locates it in patience, outside options, timing, or information.
bargaining.recognize_in_new_work: Look for surplus division, alternating offers, take-it-or-leave-it offers, or incomplete information about values.
bargaining.why_it_matters: Bargaining matters because many strategic problems are neither pure conflict nor pure cooperation. There is surplus from agreement, but the division of that surplus depends on patience, outside options, timing, and information.
bargaining.what_breaks_without_it: Without bargaining theory, the course could say agreement is efficient but not explain who gets what or why delay occurs. It would miss how threat points and waiting costs shape the split.
bargaining.naive_problem: A naive approach assumes the surplus is split fairly or evenly. The course asks what each side can credibly demand, reject, wait for, or walk away to.
bargaining.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when equal division ignores asymmetric patience or outside options. A player who can wait longer, or who has a better fallback, can change the strategic pressure of negotiation.
bargaining.lecture_emphasis: The bargaining lectures make surplus division a strategic problem rather than a moral intuition. Offers, rejections, and delay are actions with payoffs, not just conversation moves.
bargaining.cross_course_connections: Bargaining connects payoff mapping to backward induction, discounting, and private information. It also links to mechanisms because rules and outside options shape what agreements are incentive-compatible.
bargaining.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version treats negotiation as strategic surplus division. The parties may both prefer agreement to disagreement, but they disagree about the split. Offers, rejections, delay, outside options, and patience become strategic variables. The course uses bargaining to show that power is not merely personality; it often comes from credible alternatives, time costs, and information about the other side’s willingness to wait.
bargaining.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is payoff mapping plus continuation value. Each offer determines a division if accepted and a future subgame if rejected. The value of waiting or walking away sets the pressure on today’s demand.
bargaining.student_trap: Students often get stuck by assuming the fair split is the predicted split. Game theory asks what division survives incentives, not what division sounds fair from outside the model.
bargaining.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because surplus division depends on strategic alternatives, not only on the size of the surplus. Offers, rejection payoffs, delay costs, and outside options must be represented together. Bargaining models create that object so division can be explained by incentives rather than asserted fairness.
bargaining.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the source of bargaining power. If outside options, patience, information, or commitment are modeled wrongly, the predicted split can look precise while resting on fragile inputs. The boundary matters in applications because observed delay can come from strategic waiting, private information, transaction costs, or changing outside options. The bargaining model clarifies one mechanism, but the analyst still has to identify which pressure is active.

finitely_repeated_games.everyday_problem: The problem is whether repeating a game for a known number of rounds changes behavior relative to playing once.
finitely_repeated_games.first_principles_reason: Finite repetition exists because the end of the relationship can unravel incentives. If everyone knows the last round has no future punishment, that affects the round before it, and so on.
finitely_repeated_games.mathematical_object: The object is a stage game repeated T times with a known final period.
finitely_repeated_games.operation: Solve the last period first, then reason backward through earlier periods when the stage-game equilibrium is unique or when future incentives collapse.
finitely_repeated_games.worked_mini_example: If two firms know they will compete for exactly ten days, cheating on day ten cannot be punished on day eleven. That can make day nine punishment less credible too.
finitely_repeated_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to assume repetition automatically creates cooperation. A known last round can destroy that logic.
finitely_repeated_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for known horizons and unraveling arguments that start at the final period.
finitely_repeated_games.why_it_matters: Finitely repeated games matter because they teach a negative lesson: repeating a game does not automatically create cooperation. If the last round is known, the absence of future punishment can unravel incentives backward.
finitely_repeated_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without finite repetition, students might overgeneralize from ongoing relationships and assume history always disciplines behavior. The course needs the finite case to show why the endpoint is strategically powerful.
finitely_repeated_games.naive_problem: A naive approach says playing more than once should build trust. The course asks whether there is a final period where trust no longer has future consequences.
finitely_repeated_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the last round has the one-shot equilibrium, making the next-to-last round lose its punishment threat, and so on backward through the game.
finitely_repeated_games.lecture_emphasis: The finite-repetition lecture uses backward logic to make the endpoint visible. The surprise is that many rounds can behave like one round when everyone knows exactly when the relationship ends.
