finitely_repeated_games.cross_course_connections: Finite repetition connects backward induction to infinite repetition. It is the contrast case that makes discounting and no-known-final-round assumptions meaningful later.
finitely_repeated_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version is a lesson about known endings. Repeating a stage game may seem like it should allow punishment and trust, but if the final period is known, the last period has no later punishment. If the last period unravels to the one-shot equilibrium, the next-to-last period can lose its punishment power too, and the logic can roll backward.
finitely_repeated_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is backward induction applied across periods. The terminal period anchors the continuation value, and earlier periods inherit that value. A fixed horizon can therefore turn future discipline into an empty promise near the end.
finitely_repeated_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by counting repetitions rather than asking whether the relationship has a strategic future at each date. Ten known rounds and an ongoing relationship are different objects.
finitely_repeated_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because a known horizon changes every period’s incentives. The model needs to preserve the number of remaining rounds so last-period logic can be pulled backward. A finite repeated game is not just many one-shot games; it is a time-indexed strategic object.
finitely_repeated_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the known endpoint. The finite repeated-game unraveling logic changes when the horizon is uncertain, reputational types exist, or players cannot observe deviations. The classroom value of the finite case is that it blocks a lazy intuition about repetition. More rounds do not automatically mean more cooperation; what matters is whether each round still has a future consequence that can discipline current behavior. That backward pressure is the lecture’s main warning about finite horizons.

infinitely_repeated_games.everyday_problem: The problem is how cooperation can survive when each player is tempted to grab a short-run gain by cheating.
infinitely_repeated_games.first_principles_reason: Infinite repetition exists because no fixed last round means future punishment can always matter. The future becomes a strategic asset.
infinitely_repeated_games.mathematical_object: The object is a repeated game with continuation payoffs and a discount factor that measures patience.
infinitely_repeated_games.operation: Compare the one-time gain from deviation with the discounted future loss from punishment. Cooperation can hold when the future loss is large enough.
infinitely_repeated_games.worked_mini_example: A firm may want to undercut a cartel price today, but if that triggers years of price wars, the short-run gain may not be worth it.
infinitely_repeated_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to say infinite means literally forever. The model often means no known last round or a continuing relationship with future value.
infinitely_repeated_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for trigger strategies, continuation values, and inequalities comparing temptation today to punishment tomorrow.
infinitely_repeated_games.why_it_matters: Infinitely repeated games matter because they show how the future can become an enforcement device. Cooperation can be rational when the discounted loss from future punishment is larger than the immediate gain from cheating.
infinitely_repeated_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without infinite repetition, the course would lack the clean model where ongoing relationships sustain behavior that fails in a one-shot interaction. It would also miss why patience is a strategic parameter.
infinitely_repeated_games.naive_problem: A naive approach says cooperation comes from kindness or habit. The course asks whether the payoff inequality makes cooperation privately optimal when future punishment is included.
infinitely_repeated_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when players are impatient or punishment is weak. Repetition helps only if the future is valuable enough and deviations can be answered credibly.
infinitely_repeated_games.lecture_emphasis: The infinite-repetition lecture turns reputation-like discipline into a payoff comparison. Trigger strategies are not moral stories; they are continuation plans that change the value of deviating today.
infinitely_repeated_games.cross_course_connections: Infinite repetition connects finite horizons, folk theorem logic, implicit cartels, discounting, and subgame perfection. The same credibility question reappears, now stretched over an ongoing relationship.
infinitely_repeated_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version removes the known last round so the future can discipline the present. A player considering a deviation compares the one-period gain from cheating with the discounted stream of losses after punishment. Cooperation is not assumed; it must satisfy that inequality. The model often means an ongoing relationship or no known final date, not a metaphysical claim that play literally lasts forever.
infinitely_repeated_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is a present value comparison. Future payoffs are weighted by powers of the discount factor. A trigger strategy works only when the discounted punishment loss is large enough to offset the immediate deviation gain.
infinitely_repeated_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by thinking infinite repetition guarantees cooperation. If players are impatient, cannot observe deviations, or cannot punish credibly, the cooperative path may fail.
infinitely_repeated_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because ongoing relationships make future consequences part of current payoff. The discount factor and continuation payoff let the course compare today’s temptation with tomorrow’s punishment. Without that object, “the future matters” would remain a slogan rather than an inequality.
infinitely_repeated_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is enforceability of the future. Infinite repetition does not help if punishment cannot be observed, is not credible, or is discounted too heavily. The lecture use is therefore conditional: first identify the continuation value, then ask whether the proposed punishment can actually be carried out. If either piece is missing, the phrase repeated relationship is not enough to support cooperation. The lecture also uses this topic to separate mathematical infinity from economic continuation. What matters for incentives is not a calendar that literally never ends, but the absence of a commonly known final moment at which punishment loses force.

folk_theorem.everyday_problem: The problem is explaining why repeated interaction can support many outcomes, not just the one-shot equilibrium.
folk_theorem.first_principles_reason: The folk theorem exists because patient players can use future punishment to make many feasible payoff promises credible.
folk_theorem.mathematical_object: The object is a set of feasible and individually rational payoffs that can be sustained by equilibrium strategies when the discount factor is high enough.
folk_theorem.operation: Check whether the target payoff can be produced by actions, whether each player gets at least their punishment value, and whether deviations are deterred by future consequences.
folk_theorem.worked_mini_example: If two firms can both earn more by keeping prices high, the folk theorem logic says this can be sustained if cheating leads to harsh enough future competition and the firms are patient.
folk_theorem.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to read the folk theorem as predicting one outcome. It often says many outcomes are possible, which is powerful but also less predictive.
folk_theorem.recognize_in_new_work: Look for repeated-game papers showing a large set of sustainable payoffs under patience and punishment.
folk_theorem.why_it_matters: The folk theorem matters because it reveals both the power and the looseness of repeated interaction. When players are patient, many payoff patterns can be sustained, so repeated-game logic can explain cooperation but may not uniquely predict which cooperation occurs.
folk_theorem.what_breaks_without_it: Without the folk theorem, students may think repeated games merely select one cooperative equilibrium. The theorem shows a much larger set of feasible, individually rational outcomes supported by punishment.
folk_theorem.naive_problem: A naive approach looks for the cooperative outcome. The course asks which feasible payoffs can be supported once future punishment is strong enough, and that set can be surprisingly broad.
folk_theorem.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when it ignores individual rationality or feasible payoffs. Punishment can support only outcomes players prefer to their punishment value and that the stage game can actually generate.
folk_theorem.lecture_emphasis: The folk-theorem lecture is a warning as much as a result. It teaches that repeated interaction expands what equilibrium can sustain, but that expansion can reduce predictive sharpness.
folk_theorem.cross_course_connections: The folk theorem connects infinite repetition, discounting, punishment, and cartel applications. It also motivates institutional detail because equilibrium multiplicity often needs context to choose among possible outcomes.
folk_theorem.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version shows that patient repeated games can sustain a wide set of outcomes. The target payoff must be feasible from stage-game actions and individually rational relative to the punishment each player can guarantee. If those conditions hold and players care enough about the future, equilibrium strategies can often support the target through rewards and punishments. The result is powerful because it expands what is possible, but it also weakens uniqueness.
folk_theorem.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is incentive compatibility over continuation payoffs. A proposed payoff vector must give each player enough value that deviation plus punishment is worse than staying on the path. The theorem describes a set, not a single prediction.
folk_theorem.student_trap: Students often get stuck by reading the folk theorem as “cooperation happens.” The deeper message is multiplicity: many outcomes can happen, so institutions and history may be needed to select one.
folk_theorem.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because repeated games can support sets of payoffs rather than one obvious outcome. Feasibility, individual rationality, and patience define which payoff vectors can be sustained. The theorem needs that set-based object to explain both possibility and multiplicity.
folk_theorem.course_boundary_note: The boundary is prediction. The folk theorem shows many payoffs can be sustained; it does not by itself select which one will occur in a specific institution. The boundary is selection. The theorem tells the course that many outcomes can be made stable, but a real application still needs institutions, norms, history, or communication to explain why one equilibrium rather than another is chosen.

implicit_cartels.everyday_problem: The problem is how firms might keep prices high without signing an explicit cartel agreement.
implicit_cartels.first_principles_reason: Implicit cartels exist because repeated market interaction can make cheating costly. A firm may avoid undercutting today because rivals can punish tomorrow.
implicit_cartels.mathematical_object: The object is a repeated oligopoly game comparing collusive profits, deviation profits, and future punishment profits.
implicit_cartels.operation: Write the incentive constraint: the value of cooperating must be at least the one-time gain from cheating plus the discounted value after punishment.
implicit_cartels.worked_mini_example: A gas station can cut price today and steal customers, but nearby stations may respond with a price war. Tacit collusion asks when fear of that future makes quiet cooperation stable.
implicit_cartels.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to assume high prices prove explicit agreement. Repeated-game incentives can sometimes generate similar outcomes without a formal contract.
implicit_cartels.recognize_in_new_work: Look for industries with repeated price interaction, observability of deviations, and credible punishment paths.
implicit_cartels.why_it_matters: Implicit cartels matter because they show repeated-game theory inside markets. Firms may sustain high prices without an explicit contract when future punishment makes undercutting unattractive.
implicit_cartels.what_breaks_without_it: Without the cartel application, repeated-game ideas could feel abstract. The course would miss how continuation values, monitoring, and punishment shape real pricing incentives and antitrust concerns.
implicit_cartels.naive_problem: A naive approach says collusion requires a written agreement. The course asks whether firms can coordinate tacitly through repeated interaction and credible punishment.
implicit_cartels.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when it looks only at the one-period gain from cutting price. The repeated-game calculation also includes the price war or punishment that may follow.
implicit_cartels.lecture_emphasis: The cartel lecture translates discounting and trigger strategies into industrial organization. The central question is whether future lost profit is large enough to deter today deviation.
implicit_cartels.cross_course_connections: Implicit cartels connect infinite repetition, folk theorem logic, incentive compatibility, and market design. They also show where strategic cooperation can be socially harmful rather than beneficial.
implicit_cartels.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version applies repeated-game discipline to firms. A firm may want to cut price today, but if rivals respond with future low prices, the deviation can be unprofitable. The cartel is implicit when no explicit contract is needed; the strategic structure itself supplies discipline through monitoring and punishment. This also shows why cooperation among firms can be socially harmful even when cooperation sounded good in prisoner’s dilemma examples.
implicit_cartels.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is the same deviation inequality from repeated games, translated into profit. The gain from undercutting today is compared with the discounted loss from future price competition.
implicit_cartels.student_trap: Students often get stuck by equating collusion with communication. The model can produce tacit collusion if prices, market shares, or other signals let firms detect and punish deviations.
implicit_cartels.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because tacit collusion depends on a comparison across time. The model must represent the current profit from cheating and the discounted loss from future punishment. That object turns cartel stability into an incentive constraint instead of a story about firms being friendly.
implicit_cartels.course_boundary_note: The boundary is monitoring and legality. Tacit collusion requires that firms can detect deviations and respond; market noise, entry, and antitrust constraints can break the mechanism. In lecture terms, the important boundary is that the model is explaining an incentive mechanism, not proving that firms actually coordinated in any given market. Evidence about prices, demand shocks, communication, and monitoring would be needed before applying the concept outside the classroom example. The concept also depends on market observability. If firms cannot tell whether a low price came from cheating, demand noise, cost shocks, or a new entrant, punishment may be too blunt or too costly to sustain the cartel path.

imperfect_competition.everyday_problem: The problem is that many real markets sit between a street market with countless sellers and a single monopolist. A firm may be large enough that its price or quantity choice moves the market, but it still has rivals whose choices push back.
imperfect_competition.first_principles_reason: Imperfect competition exists because scarcity, location, patents, brands, search costs, and product differences can give firms market power. Once a firm is not a pure price taker, its action affects demand, rival payoffs, and its own profit, so ordinary one-person maximization is no longer enough.
imperfect_competition.mathematical_object: The object is a profit function for each firm, such as price minus cost times quantity, together with a best-response rule that says which quantity or price is most profitable against rival behavior.
imperfect_competition.operation: Write how total market demand depends on price or quantity, assign each firm a cost, then ask what each firm wants to do given the other firm's action. Cournot uses quantity choices; Bertrand uses price choices.
imperfect_competition.worked_mini_example: Two nearby coffee shops both choose how much to sell or what price to charge. If one shop raises price, some customers leave; if one shop expands quantity, the market price may fall. The best choice is therefore not just a cost calculation. It depends on the rival's choice and on how customers respond.
imperfect_competition.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat imperfect competition as just monopoly with more firms. The whole point is that each firm has some power but not complete power. The strategic object is the interaction among firms, not only the demand curve facing one seller.
imperfect_competition.recognize_in_new_work: Look for a model where firms choose prices, quantities, entry, capacity, or product features while knowing that rivals' actions change the payoff. If the paper asks for a best response by a firm rather than a single optimal monopoly price, this concept is active.
imperfect_competition.why_it_matters: Imperfect competition matters because it explains markups, undercutting, entry, quantity competition, and why market outcomes can differ from both perfect competition and monopoly. It is the bridge from payoff tables to economic applications where firms are strategic players.
imperfect_competition.what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the course could not explain why a firm may charge above cost, why price competition can be brutal, or why changing the modeling choice from quantity to price can change the prediction. Market behavior would be described as if firms either had no power or total power.
imperfect_competition.naive_problem: A naive approach says a firm should choose the price or quantity that maximizes profit from a fixed demand curve. The lecture shows why that is incomplete: when other firms are present, the demand and payoff consequences depend on their choices too.
imperfect_competition.failed_simple_approach: The simple monopoly approach fails when rivals can respond. A price that looks profitable in isolation may lose the market to an undercutting rival, while a quantity that looks safe may lower the price once another firm produces too.
imperfect_competition.lecture_emphasis: The imperfect-competition lecture deliberately moves from demand and monopoly markup into game theory. The teaching point is that market power creates a strategic profit problem: once multiple firms matter, the course must talk about best responses rather than a single firm's isolated optimum.
imperfect_competition.cross_course_connections: Imperfect competition connects strategic-form games, best response, Nash equilibrium, implicit cartels, and one-shot deviation. The Cournot and Bertrand contrast also previews why model representation matters: changing the action from quantity to price can change the strategic prediction.
imperfect_competition.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version starts from two extremes. In perfect competition, one seller is too small to move price. In monopoly, one seller faces the whole market alone. Imperfect competition is the middle case: a few firms have market power, so their own choices affect price or demand, but rivals still matter. That is why the lecture can begin with demand curves and markups but eventually has to introduce Cournot and Bertrand models. The mathematical move is to turn a market into a game among firms. Each firm has a payoff formula, and each payoff depends on both its own action and the rival's action.
imperfect_competition.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is strategic profit maximization. Profit is not just revenue minus cost; in these models, revenue depends on the market price, and the market price depends on the total choices of firms. A best-response curve records the quantity or price that maximizes one firm's profit for each rival action.
imperfect_competition.student_trap: Students often get stuck by mixing up the market story with the strategic object. The story may be coffee shops, patents, or internet providers, but the object is the payoff map from firm choices to profits.
imperfect_competition.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because words like competition and market power are too loose. The model must say what firms choose, how choices determine price or demand, and how profit changes when rivals act. Best responses make the strategic dependence explicit.
imperfect_competition.course_boundary_note: The boundary is model specification. Cournot and Bertrand are not universal laws of competition; they are different ways to represent what firms choose. The lecture itself flags this by contrasting quantity choice and price choice. In real markets, capacity constraints, product differentiation, search frictions, contracts, and regulation can change which representation fits. The concept is strongest when the analyst can defend why price, quantity, entry, or another action is the strategic variable.

bayesian_games.everyday_problem: The problem is strategic choice when players do not know exactly who they are facing or what payoffs the other side has.
bayesian_games.first_principles_reason: Bayesian games exist because private information changes best responses. A player must choose against a distribution of possible types, not a single known opponent.
bayesian_games.mathematical_object: The object is a game with types, priors over types, actions for each type, and payoff functions that may depend on type.
bayesian_games.operation: List each possible type, assign prior probabilities, define strategies as type-contingent plans, and compute expected payoffs given beliefs.
bayesian_games.worked_mini_example: A bidder may not know whether rivals value the object highly or weakly. Their bid must respond to that uncertainty, not to one known payoff table.
bayesian_games.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat hidden information as random noise outside the game. In Bayesian games, the uncertainty is part of the strategic structure.
bayesian_games.recognize_in_new_work: Look for models with types, priors, private values, costs, signals, or asymmetric information.
bayesian_games.why_it_matters: Bayesian games matter because private information changes what strategy even means. A strategy must often specify what each possible type would do, while opponents choose using beliefs over those types.
bayesian_games.what_breaks_without_it: Without Bayesian games, the course would treat hidden values, costs, and motives as if everyone knew them. Auctions, signaling, and incomplete-information bargaining would collapse into misleading complete-information models.
bayesian_games.naive_problem: A naive approach says players are uncertain and stops there. The course asks what the hidden types are, what probabilities players assign to them, and how payoffs depend on those types.
bayesian_games.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when one action is optimal against one type but not another. The player is choosing against a probability distribution, not a single known opponent.
bayesian_games.lecture_emphasis: The Bayesian-game lecture makes uncertainty part of the game form. Types, priors, and type-contingent strategies become the representation before equilibrium is even checked.
bayesian_games.cross_course_connections: Bayesian games connect expected utility to Bayesian Nash, auctions, signaling, and PBE. They are the private-information foundation for the final third of the course.
bayesian_games.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version changes the game form by adding hidden types. A player may know their own value, cost, or payoff parameter while others only hold beliefs. Strategies must now specify actions for each type, because a high-value bidder and low-value bidder may rationally behave differently. The course uses this representation before solving equilibrium because the private information itself is part of the strategic environment.
bayesian_games.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is expected utility over types. A player chooses an action or plan while averaging over the possible hidden states they do not observe. Priors define the probability weights before actions reveal anything.
bayesian_games.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating uncertainty as noise outside the model. In a Bayesian game, uncertainty is inside the model and has named objects: types, beliefs, strategies, and payoffs.
bayesian_games.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because hidden information changes the identity of the decision problem. Types and priors let the model represent what each player knows privately and what others believe. Without them, private values and costs would be invisible to the equilibrium calculation.
bayesian_games.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the type model. If the type space, priors, or payoff dependence are wrong, Bayesian equilibrium can be internally consistent but externally misleading. The lecture boundary also explains why the type space is a modeling choice. Too few types can erase important private information; too many can make the model flexible without adding insight. The useful type structure is the one that carries the strategic uncertainty actually driving behavior. The model’s usefulness depends on naming that hidden structure carefully.

types_and_beliefs.everyday_problem: The problem is keeping track of hidden facts and what players think those facts might be.
types_and_beliefs.first_principles_reason: Types and beliefs exist because private information has to be represented somewhere. A type stores what one player knows; a belief stores what others think is likely.
types_and_beliefs.mathematical_object: The object is a type space plus probability beliefs over types or histories.
types_and_beliefs.operation: Assign each privately informed player a type, specify what that type changes, and write beliefs about which type has been drawn.
types_and_beliefs.worked_mini_example: In an auction, a bidder's value is their type. Other bidders do not see it, but they hold beliefs about the distribution of possible values.
types_and_beliefs.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to blur type and action. A type is hidden information; an action is a choice that may reveal or conceal it.
types_and_beliefs.recognize_in_new_work: Look for any model where behavior depends on values, costs, quality, or information that only one side observes.
types_and_beliefs.why_it_matters: Types and beliefs matter because they split hidden information into two objects: what the world could be and what players think the world could be. That separation keeps uncertainty from becoming a vague verbal patch.
types_and_beliefs.what_breaks_without_it: Without types and beliefs, private-information models would not say who knows what or how uncertainty enters payoffs. The analyst could not distinguish a high-value bidder from a low-value bidder or a receiver belief from sender truth.
types_and_beliefs.naive_problem: A naive approach says one player has information. The course asks what exact private fact is being represented as a type and what probability story others hold about it.
types_and_beliefs.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when beliefs are treated as facts. A receiver may believe a sender is high type, but that belief must be updated and tested against incentives.
types_and_beliefs.lecture_emphasis: The lecture uses types and beliefs to make asymmetric information inspectable. The important teaching move is that uncertainty becomes a model component, not a footnote.
types_and_beliefs.cross_course_connections: Types and beliefs connect Bayesian games, Bayesian Nash, auctions, signaling, cheap talk, and PBE. They are also the reason expected utility keeps reappearing in private-information settings.
types_and_beliefs.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version separates the hidden fact from the probability story about that fact. A type is the private information that changes payoffs or available actions. A belief is another player’s probability distribution over possible types or states. This distinction is crucial because a sender may know the type while a receiver only has a belief, and strategic behavior can be designed to change that belief.
types_and_beliefs.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is a state space with probability weights. The type indexes which payoff function or information situation is true; the belief says how likely each index seems to another player. Updating changes the weights after observations.
types_and_beliefs.student_trap: Students often get stuck by saying “the player believes the type” as if belief and type were the same thing. One is the hidden state; the other is someone’s uncertain view of it.
types_and_beliefs.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because uncertainty has two sides: the hidden state and someone’s probability over it. Types represent the state; beliefs represent the uncertainty. Keeping them separate lets the course analyze signaling, updating, and type-contingent strategy without confusing truth with perception.
types_and_beliefs.course_boundary_note: The boundary is discipline on beliefs. Beliefs are necessary, but they should come from priors, signals, observations, or equilibrium restrictions rather than being chosen to rescue any story. The lecture boundary is that beliefs should be inspectable. A model that can support any action by inventing a convenient belief has stopped explaining. The belief structure must connect to priors, information, or equilibrium restrictions.

bayesian_nash_equilibrium.everyday_problem: The problem is predicting behavior when each possible type of a player may want a different action.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.first_principles_reason: Bayesian Nash exists because equilibrium must be checked before hidden information is revealed to others. Each type needs its own best response under beliefs.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.mathematical_object: The object is a strategy for every type of every player, where each type maximizes expected payoff given beliefs about other types and their strategies.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.operation: For each type, hold fixed the strategy rules of other players, average over unknown types, and check whether that type wants to change its prescribed action.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.worked_mini_example: In a first-price auction, a high-value bidder and low-value bidder follow different bidding rules. BNE checks that each value type is bidding optimally against the distribution of rival values.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to look for one action per player. In Bayesian Nash, a strategy is a rule mapping types to actions.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.recognize_in_new_work: Look for type-contingent strategies and expected-payoff best response conditions.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.why_it_matters: Bayesian Nash equilibrium matters because it extends strategic stability to hidden-information settings. Each type must be willing to follow its plan given beliefs about other players types and strategies.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.what_breaks_without_it: Without Bayesian Nash, the course could define types and beliefs but not check whether type-contingent strategies hold together. A proposed bidding or action rule might fail for one hidden type even if it sounds plausible overall.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.naive_problem: A naive approach asks whether the average player wants to deviate. The course asks whether every relevant type wants to deviate under the beliefs and payoff consequences facing that type.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when pooling all types hides profitable deviations. A high-value bidder and a low-value bidder may face different incentives even under the same auction rule.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.lecture_emphasis: The Bayesian-Nash lecture teaches equilibrium as a plan for each type. Stability is checked in expected payoff terms because each type responds to beliefs about others hidden information.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.cross_course_connections: Bayesian Nash connects Nash equilibrium to expected utility, types, beliefs, and auctions. PBE later adds timing and belief updating after observed histories.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version extends Nash by asking every type to pass the best-response test. A strategy is no longer just one action for a player; it is a rule assigning actions to that player’s possible types. Equilibrium requires that each type, given beliefs about other players’ types and strategies, has no profitable deviation in expected payoff terms.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is mutual consistency across type-contingent plans. For each type, hold fixed the strategy rules of others and the belief distribution over their types, then maximize expected payoff. Every type must be content with its assigned action.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.student_trap: Students often get stuck by checking only the average player. Bayesian Nash is stricter: a proposed strategy can fail because one particular type wants to deviate, even if the pooled behavior looks reasonable.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because hidden types need their own stability checks. A single action per player is not enough; each possible type needs a plan, and each plan must be optimal in expectation. Bayesian Nash equilibrium formalizes mutual consistency across those type-indexed plans.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium.course_boundary_note: The boundary is timing and updating. Bayesian Nash handles static type uncertainty, but dynamic signals and histories require belief systems such as PBE. The boundary is why Bayesian Nash is not the final word for signaling games. It handles plans by type before dynamic observations, but once actions reveal information over time, equilibrium must also discipline posterior beliefs. Each type receives its own incentive audit, not just the player as a whole.

screening_and_adverse_selection.everyday_problem: The problem is that a price or offer can change who shows up. A seller, insurer, or bargainer may set a rule thinking about an average customer, but the people who accept are not average; they are selected by the rule itself.
screening_and_adverse_selection.first_principles_reason: Screening and adverse selection exist because one side has hidden information about value, cost, quality, health, or risk. The uninformed side can only offer terms, and those terms filter the informed side. That filtering changes the group being served.
screening_and_adverse_selection.mathematical_object: The object is an expected payoff under a cutoff rule: a price or offer is accepted only by types for whom accepting is better than rejecting, so the distribution of accepted types changes with the price.
screening_and_adverse_selection.operation: Name the hidden type, write the participation condition for each type, compute which types accept the offer, then recompute the payoff using only that selected group. The key operation is updating the composition of participants after the rule is announced.
screening_and_adverse_selection.worked_mini_example: An insurer sets one price for a policy. People who expect low medical costs may walk away, while people who expect high costs are more likely to buy. Raising the price can bring in a worse risk pool, so the insurer cannot reason from the average person before the price was set.
screening_and_adverse_selection.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat demand as only fewer people buying when price rises. In adverse selection, the identity of the buyers changes too, and that composition change can matter more than the number of buyers.
screening_and_adverse_selection.recognize_in_new_work: Look for models where an offer, price, contract, or test makes different hidden types sort themselves. If changing the rule changes the pool of participants, the screening/adverse-selection primitive is active.
screening_and_adverse_selection.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it explains delay, disagreement, insurance problems, used-good markets, and bargaining failures even when trade would create value under full information. It shows why hidden information can block mutually beneficial exchange.
screening_and_adverse_selection.what_breaks_without_it: Without this concept, the course would predict trade whenever buyer value exceeds seller cost. It would miss the reason some trades fail: the terms that attract one type may drive away another or reveal information that changes future bargaining.
screening_and_adverse_selection.naive_problem: A naive approach says that if there are gains from trade, the parties should immediately agree on some price between cost and value. Lecture 23 shows why that can fail when value, cost, quality, or risk is privately known.
screening_and_adverse_selection.failed_simple_approach: The complete-information bargaining model fails because offers can carry information and because acceptance is selective. Once an offer filters types, the uninformed side is no longer facing the original population.
screening_and_adverse_selection.lecture_emphasis: The bargaining-with-incomplete-information lecture contrasts complete-information bargaining, where agreement is immediate when gains from trade exist, with hidden-information bargaining, where offers can screen types and create delay or disagreement.
screening_and_adverse_selection.cross_course_connections: Screening and adverse selection connect Bayesian games, types and beliefs, bargaining, signaling, auctions, and PBE. Signaling asks what a privately informed first mover reveals through action; screening asks how an uninformed first mover designs a rule that makes hidden types reveal themselves by accepting or rejecting.
screening_and_adverse_selection.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version begins with the clean complete-information benchmark: if the buyer value exceeds seller cost, there is room for a price that helps both sides, so agreement should happen without delay. Incomplete information breaks that logic. A price or offer does not merely divide surplus; it also sorts types. In insurance, people who buy at a given price are the people for whom the product is worth at least that price, and those people may be the most expensive to serve. In bargaining, an offer or rejection can reveal something about value or cost. The mathematical lesson is that the payoff must be computed after selection, not before.
screening_and_adverse_selection.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is conditional composition. Start with a population of possible types. A rule selects a subset of those types. The payoff calculation must use the selected subset, because the rule itself changed who participates.
screening_and_adverse_selection.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating hidden information as just another probability. The lecture point is sharper: the action or price changes which hidden types remain in the game, so the probability distribution after participation is not the original distribution.
screening_and_adverse_selection.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because ordinary average reasoning lies in selected populations. A cutoff, participation condition, or posterior distribution is needed to say who accepts, who rejects, and what the uninformed side should believe after observing that choice.
screening_and_adverse_selection.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the source of selection. Not every failed trade is adverse selection; the mechanism requires hidden type information and terms that select different types differently. The evidence supports the screening/adverse-selection logic in the lecture's buyer-seller and insurance examples. Broader claims about real insurance or legal bargaining require evidence about actual information, costs, offers, and participation.

auctions.everyday_problem: The problem is allocating an object when people know their own values but the seller and rival bidders may not.
auctions.first_principles_reason: Auctions exist because rules can make private information compete in public. Bids are actions shaped by values, beliefs, payment rules, and competition.
auctions.mathematical_object: The object is an auction mechanism: bidder values, bid spaces, allocation rules, and payment rules.
auctions.operation: Specify who wins for each bid profile, what they pay, and how each bidder trades off a higher chance of winning against a worse price.
auctions.worked_mini_example: In a first-price auction, a bidder who values the object at 100 faces two forces. Bidding closer to 100 makes winning more likely, but if they win at 100 they keep no surplus. Bidding 70 leaves surplus if they win, but risks losing to someone they might have beaten. The bid is therefore not a direct confession of value. It is a strategic choice shaped by the payment rule and beliefs about rival bids. In a second-price auction the same value can create different incentives because the winner pays someone else bid.
auctions.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to think the highest-value bidder automatically bids their value in every auction format.
auctions.recognize_in_new_work: Look for allocation and payment rules that transform private values into strategic bids.
auctions.why_it_matters: Auctions matter because they show how rules translate private values into strategic bids. The course uses them to move from predicting behavior under rules to designing rules that produce allocation, revenue, or information goals.
auctions.what_breaks_without_it: Without auction theory, the course would miss one of the clearest economic applications of incomplete-information games. It could not explain bid shading, truthful bidding in special formats, or why payment rules change behavior.
auctions.naive_problem: A naive approach says the person who values the object most should simply bid that value. The course asks how the payment rule changes the incentive to reveal or shade that value.
auctions.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails in first-price auctions, where bidding full value leaves no surplus if the bidder wins. Strategic bidding balances winning probability against the price paid.
auctions.lecture_emphasis: The auction lecture makes mechanism design concrete. Bids are not raw values; they are strategic reports shaped by beliefs about rivals and by the rule mapping bids to payments.
auctions.cross_course_connections: Auctions connect Bayesian games, expected utility, incentive compatibility, and revenue equivalence. Ad auctions extend the same logic when platforms allocate ranked positions rather than a single object.
auctions.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version treats an auction as a rule system that turns hidden values into public actions. A seller wants to allocate an object and collect payment, but bidders know more about their own willingness to pay than the seller does. The auction format tells bidders how bids map to allocation and payment. That mapping changes behavior. First-price rules make bidders care directly about the price they name; second-price rules separate the winning bid from the payment in a way that can make truthful bidding attractive under standard assumptions. The lecture evidence about bid deviations matters because auctions are evaluated by the deviations participants want to make, not by the designer desired story.
auctions.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is expected payoff from bidding. A bid affects the probability of winning and the payment if winning occurs. The bidder chooses the bid that balances those two forces against beliefs about rival bids or values.
auctions.student_trap: Students often get stuck by treating bids as direct value reports. In many auctions, bids are strategic actions distorted by payment rules, risk, competition, and beliefs about rivals.
auctions.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because allocation and payment cannot be analyzed separately. A high bid changes the probability of winning and may also change the amount paid. A bidder compares expected surplus, not just the thrill of winning. The model therefore needs values, bid spaces, allocation rules, payment rules, beliefs about competitors, and payoff comparisons. Without that combined object, the analyst cannot tell whether a bid reports value, shades value, or strategically distorts information.
auctions.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the value and information environment. Private values, common values, risk aversion, budget limits, reserve prices, entry costs, collusion, and correlated signals can all change bidding logic. A revenue or truthfulness claim that is correct in one auction model may fail after one of those assumptions changes. The practical reading rule is: never interpret a bid until you know the payment rule and what bidders know.

revenue_equivalence.everyday_problem: The problem is comparing auction formats that look different: first-price, second-price, English, and others may create different bidding behavior.
revenue_equivalence.first_principles_reason: Revenue equivalence exists because different rules can sometimes generate the same expected payment once bidders adjust their strategies.
revenue_equivalence.mathematical_object: The object is a theorem linking allocation rules and expected payments under assumptions such as risk neutrality, independent private values, and symmetric bidders.
revenue_equivalence.operation: Check whether the auction gives the object to the same type of bidder and gives the lowest type the same expected payoff; then expected revenue can coincide.
revenue_equivalence.worked_mini_example: First-price and second-price auctions induce different bids, but under the theorem's assumptions the seller's expected revenue can match because bidders strategically shade in one format and bid truthfully in another.
revenue_equivalence.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to quote revenue equivalence without the assumptions. Change risk, affiliation, reserve prices, or asymmetry and the result can fail.
revenue_equivalence.recognize_in_new_work: Look for auction comparisons where allocation sameness and bidder payoff normalization drive payment conclusions.
revenue_equivalence.why_it_matters: Revenue equivalence matters because it teaches students to look past surface format. Different auction rules can produce the same expected seller revenue when allocation rules and assumptions line up in the right way.
revenue_equivalence.what_breaks_without_it: Without revenue equivalence, every auction comparison would be treated as an isolated case. The course would miss the deeper structure that makes some formats equivalent and the assumptions that make equivalence fragile.
revenue_equivalence.naive_problem: A naive approach says first-price and second-price auctions must differ because their payment rules look different. The theorem asks whether strategic bid adjustment offsets that difference in expectation.
revenue_equivalence.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when it compares rules while holding bids fixed. Bidders change their bids when the rule changes, so revenue comparison must include the equilibrium response.
revenue_equivalence.lecture_emphasis: The revenue-equivalence lecture is about assumptions doing work. The theorem is powerful because it says exactly when format differences wash out, and informative because it shows when they will not.
revenue_equivalence.cross_course_connections: Revenue equivalence connects auctions, Bayesian Nash, expected payments, and incentive compatibility. It also prepares students to read mechanism papers by checking distributional and valuation assumptions before trusting a revenue claim.
revenue_equivalence.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version asks why very different auction rules can sometimes give the seller the same expected revenue. The answer is not that the rules are identical. It is that under specific assumptions, bidders adjust strategies so that allocation probabilities and expected payments line up. This teaches students to inspect the theorem’s conditions rather than memorize a surprising slogan.
revenue_equivalence.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is that expected payment can be pinned down by allocation rules plus boundary conditions under the standard assumptions. If the same type has the same chance of winning across mechanisms, expected revenue can match even when payment timing differs.
revenue_equivalence.student_trap: Students often get stuck by comparing the rules while holding bids fixed. Equilibrium bids change with the auction format, and those strategic adjustments are exactly what the theorem accounts for.
revenue_equivalence.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because comparing auction formats requires more than comparing labels. Expected revenue depends on allocation probabilities, payment rules, and equilibrium bidding. Revenue equivalence formalizes the conditions under which those pieces line up across mechanisms.
revenue_equivalence.course_boundary_note: The boundary is the theorem assumptions. Once values are affiliated, bidders are risk averse, reserve prices change, or allocation rules differ, equivalence may fail. The teaching payoff is that failure is informative. When revenue equivalence breaks, the reason usually points to a real economic force such as risk aversion, common values, entry, asymmetry, or a changed allocation rule. The theorem is a map of assumptions as much as a revenue result.

ad_auctions.everyday_problem: The problem is selling attention slots, not a single physical object. Position affects clicks, quality affects usefulness, and bids interact with platform rules.
ad_auctions.first_principles_reason: Ad auctions exist because online markets must allocate ranked slots repeatedly and automatically while advertisers have private values per click.
ad_auctions.mathematical_object: The object is a sponsored-search mechanism combining bids, click-through rates, quality scores, allocation order, and per-click payments.
ad_auctions.operation: Rank advertisers by the platform's scoring rule, assign slots, then compute payments from the rule that determines what each advertiser must pay per click.
ad_auctions.worked_mini_example: A lower bidder with a highly relevant ad may beat a higher bidder if quality affects ranking. The mechanism is not just who writes the biggest number.
ad_auctions.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat ad auctions as ordinary one-object auctions. Position, click probability, and platform quality adjustments change the strategic object.
ad_auctions.recognize_in_new_work: Look for markets with ranked slots, click probabilities, quality scores, and generalized second-price style rules.
ad_auctions.why_it_matters: Ad auctions matter because they show auction theory under platform constraints. The object is not just an item; it is attention in ranked positions, filtered through clicks, relevance, quality scores, and advertiser value.
ad_auctions.what_breaks_without_it: Without ad auctions, the course would leave mechanism design at textbook allocation. It would miss how online markets mix bidding strategy with measurement, ranking rules, and platform incentives.
ad_auctions.naive_problem: A naive approach says the highest bid should win the top slot. The course asks whether the platform should also consider click probability, ad quality, user relevance, and long-run participation.
ad_auctions.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when a high bid on a low-quality ad produces fewer useful clicks than a lower bid on a better match. The platform is pricing attention, not only selling rank.
ad_auctions.lecture_emphasis: The ad-auction lecture shows game theory as systems design in a market. The bidding rule, ranking rule, and pricing rule jointly shape advertiser behavior.
ad_auctions.cross_course_connections: Ad auctions connect standard auctions to mechanism design, payoff mapping, Bayesian reasoning, and repeated platform participation. They also show why real institutions often add engineering details to clean theory.
ad_auctions.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version moves auction theory into platform design. The platform is allocating positions that generate clicks, not simply handing over a single object. Advertisers care about conversion value, users respond to relevance, and the platform may use quality scores or predicted click-through rates. Bidding is therefore intertwined with ranking and measurement. The clean auction object becomes a system with feedback.
ad_auctions.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is an allocation rule over ranked slots plus a payment rule per click or impression. A bidder’s payoff depends on position, click probability, value per click, price, and sometimes quality adjustments.
ad_auctions.student_trap: Students often get stuck by seeing only bids. In sponsored search, the highest bid may not create the highest platform value if relevance and click probability differ.
ad_auctions.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because platform auctions allocate attention through rankings, clicks, and quality adjustments. A simple highest-bid object misses the product being sold. The ad-auction model keeps bid, position, click probability, and value in the same incentive calculation.
ad_auctions.course_boundary_note: The boundary is platform feedback. Click predictions, quality scores, user behavior, and repeated advertiser learning can make the simple auction model only a first approximation. The lecture boundary is that real platforms update predictions and rules over time. A static ad-auction model can explain the core incentive tradeoff, but platform learning and advertiser experimentation can add dynamics that the basic mechanism does not fully capture. The platform’s ranking formula becomes part of the strategic environment.

perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.everyday_problem: The problem is dynamic play with hidden information: after observing actions, players must update beliefs and continue choosing rationally.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.first_principles_reason: PBE exists because dynamic Bayesian games need both credible continuation behavior and believable beliefs about what has happened.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.mathematical_object: The object is a strategy profile plus a belief system, with sequential rationality and belief consistency where Bayes' rule applies.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.operation: At each information set, check that the strategy is optimal given beliefs; then check that beliefs are updated consistently from the strategies whenever possible.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.worked_mini_example: In a signaling game, seeing someone choose education may change an employer's belief about worker type. PBE checks both the education choice and the employer's updated response.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to focus only on strategies and forget beliefs. In hidden-information dynamic games, beliefs are part of the equilibrium object.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.recognize_in_new_work: Look for dynamic asymmetric-information models with off-path beliefs, updating, and sequential rationality.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.why_it_matters: PBE matters because dynamic private-information games need two disciplines at once: players must act optimally after histories, and their beliefs about hidden types must be consistent with observed behavior where possible.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.what_breaks_without_it: Without PBE, signaling and other dynamic asymmetric-information models could prescribe actions without explaining the beliefs that make those actions rational. Credibility would be separated from learning.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.naive_problem: A naive approach checks the sender strategy or receiver action alone. The course asks for the whole object: strategies plus beliefs, tied together by sequential rationality and Bayesian updating when applicable.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when an off-path event occurs. Bayes rule may not determine beliefs there, but the model still has to specify beliefs carefully because they affect continuation behavior.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.lecture_emphasis: The PBE lecture is the course synthesis of time and hidden information. It repairs dynamic games by making beliefs part of the equilibrium object rather than an informal explanation after the fact.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.cross_course_connections: PBE connects extensive form, Bayesian games, types and beliefs, signaling, and subgame perfection. It is where the course asks credibility and inference to pass the same test.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version combines two repairs: dynamic credibility and belief consistency. In a signaling or other dynamic private-information game, a player’s later action depends on what they believe after observing earlier behavior. PBE therefore includes both strategies and a belief system. Strategies must be sequentially rational given beliefs, and beliefs must follow Bayes’ rule wherever the observed path gives probabilities to update from.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is a coupled object. Beliefs determine optimal continuation actions, while strategies determine which observations are likely and therefore how beliefs should update. Neither side can be checked in isolation.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.student_trap: Students often get stuck by solving the strategy profile and treating beliefs as commentary. In PBE, beliefs are part of the equilibrium data, especially because off-path beliefs can affect credibility.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because dynamic private-information games require beliefs and actions to discipline each other. Strategies say what players do; beliefs say what they infer after histories. PBE binds the two so credibility and updating are checked together.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium.course_boundary_note: The boundary is off-path freedom. PBE disciplines beliefs where Bayes rule applies, but unexpected histories can still leave multiple belief specifications and multiple equilibria. The practical reading rule is to inspect both halves of the candidate equilibrium. If the strategies look sensible but the beliefs are arbitrary, or the beliefs look plausible but the continuation actions are not optimal, the PBE claim has not been earned. Belief discipline is therefore not optional decoration. The lecture uses that discipline to keep inference and sequential choice tied together.

signaling.everyday_problem: The problem is how someone with private information can convince others of it through an observable action.
signaling.first_principles_reason: Signaling exists because words or actions can change beliefs only if different types have different incentives or costs.
signaling.mathematical_object: The object is a sender-receiver game with types, signals, receiver beliefs, and receiver actions.
signaling.operation: For each possible type, compare the payoff from sending each signal; then check how the receiver updates beliefs and responds.
signaling.worked_mini_example: A diploma can signal ability only if imitation is harder or less attractive for low-ability workers than for high-ability workers. If every worker can get the same diploma at the same cost and employers know that, the diploma should not separate types. If high-ability workers can earn it at lower cost, choosing education may be worthwhile for them and not worth mimicking for others. The receiver then treats the observable action as evidence about hidden type because the sender incentives differ by type.
signaling.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to assume any costly action is a signal. It signals only if costs and incentives differ across types in a way receivers can reason from.
signaling.recognize_in_new_work: Look for actions that are valuable mainly because observers infer hidden quality, commitment, or type from them.
signaling.why_it_matters: Signaling matters because hidden information can sometimes be communicated through costly or type-dependent action. The receiver learns not from a label but from the fact that different types face different incentives to send the signal.
signaling.what_breaks_without_it: Without signaling, the course could not explain education, warranties, investment, or other actions whose value partly comes from what observers infer. It would treat all messages as direct information rather than incentive-shaped evidence.
signaling.naive_problem: A naive approach says a signal reveals type because the sender says so or chooses it. The course asks why a low type would not imitate a high type if imitation were profitable.
signaling.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when the signal is equally cheap for all types. If every type would send it, the receiver should not infer separation from observing it.
signaling.lecture_emphasis: The signaling lecture teaches separating and pooling as incentive patterns. The signal works only when the cost, benefit, or payoff response differs enough across types.
signaling.cross_course_connections: Signaling connects Bayesian games, PBE, beliefs, incentive compatibility, and cheap talk. It is the costly-action counterpart to costless messages and the dynamic counterpart to static hidden types.
signaling.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version starts with an observation problem. The receiver sees the sender action but cannot directly see the sender private information. That gap is why a signal can matter. The action is not informative by magic; it becomes informative only after checking incentives. A separating signal requires each type to prefer its assigned signal over imitation. A pooling outcome arises when multiple types prefer the same observable action, leaving the receiver unable to distinguish them. The lecture progression from simple signaling to richer applications matters because the same hidden-information skeleton keeps reappearing: private type, observable action, receiver belief, receiver response.
signaling.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is incentive compatibility across types plus belief updating. For separation, each type must prefer its assigned signal over mimicking another type. The receiver’s posterior belief then justifies the response to each signal.
signaling.student_trap: Students often get stuck by assuming costly means informative. A costly signal is informative only if the cost or benefit differs across types in the right direction.
signaling.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because observability and truth are different. The receiver observes an action, not the private type that caused it. The model must represent type-dependent costs or benefits, the sender signal choice, the receiver posterior belief, and the receiver action. Only then can it ask whether the proposed signal survives imitation. Without the incentive constraints, a story about signaling can mistake decoration for information.
signaling.course_boundary_note: The boundary is mimicry. A signal separates types only when the wrong type does not want to copy it after accounting for cost and receiver response. Cost alone is not enough; a costly action can still be uninformative if all types pay the cost for the same benefit. The empirical question is whether the real signal actually has the type-dependent cost or payoff difference the model assumes.

cheap_talk.everyday_problem: The problem is whether costless messages can influence behavior when the speaker may want to mislead.
cheap_talk.first_principles_reason: Cheap talk exists because communication has no direct cost or binding force, so credibility must come from aligned incentives rather than from the message itself.
cheap_talk.mathematical_object: The object is a sender-receiver game where messages do not directly change payoffs but can change beliefs and actions.
cheap_talk.operation: Compare what each type of sender wants the receiver to do. If interests are aligned enough, informative messages can be credible; if not, messages may pool and reveal little.
cheap_talk.worked_mini_example: Imagine an advisor who knows which project is best and a decision maker who must choose. If both want the same project chosen, costless advice can be informative because the advisor gains by telling the truth. If the advisor always prefers the biggest project regardless of quality, every state pushes them toward the same message. The receiver should then treat the message as persuasion rather than evidence. The math is asking which messages each sender type would voluntarily send once they anticipate the receiver response.
cheap_talk.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to say cheap means irrelevant. Costless speech can matter when incentives make truthful communication self-enforcing.
cheap_talk.recognize_in_new_work: Look for models where messages are nonbinding and the key question is whether incentives allow information transmission.
cheap_talk.why_it_matters: Cheap talk matters because communication can influence behavior even when messages are costless and nonbinding, but only under incentive conditions. It teaches that speech is strategic rather than automatically informative.
cheap_talk.what_breaks_without_it: Without cheap talk, the course would treat all communication as either irrelevant noise or costly signaling. It would miss the middle case where aligned interests make some costless messages credible enough to affect actions.
cheap_talk.naive_problem: A naive approach says costless talk cannot matter because anyone can say anything. The course asks whether the sender would actually want to lie given how the receiver will respond.
cheap_talk.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when preferences are partially aligned. In those cases, a message can partition information usefully even though it carries no direct cost.
cheap_talk.lecture_emphasis: The cheap-talk lecture forces credibility to come from payoff alignment rather than signal cost. That contrast is the reason it belongs after signaling, not before private information is understood.
cheap_talk.cross_course_connections: Cheap talk connects signaling, Bayesian games, beliefs, and common knowledge. It also draws a boundary: if incentives are opposed, speech may pool; if sufficiently aligned, speech can guide receiver action.
cheap_talk.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version removes the usual crutch of cost. In signaling, an action may be credible because the wrong type finds it too expensive to imitate. Cheap talk asks what remains when messages are free and nonbinding. The sender can say anything, so credibility must come from preferences. If sender and receiver want similar actions in a region of states, a message can honestly group those states and help the receiver choose. If their interests diverge too much, different sender types may all prefer the same flattering or persuasive message, so the receiver learns little. The lecture therefore makes communication a payoff problem, not a vocabulary problem.
cheap_talk.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is partitioning information through equilibrium messages. A message can group states into regions where truthful communication is self-enforcing because the sender prefers the receiver response induced by that message.
cheap_talk.student_trap: Students often get stuck by saying cheap talk is either always useless or always informative. The lecture point is conditional: credibility depends on payoff alignment and receiver response.
cheap_talk.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because words alone do not reveal incentives. A sentence can sound informative even when every sender type would choose it. The model needs states, sender preferences, receiver actions, messages, and beliefs so it can check whether a proposed communication rule is self-enforcing. The hard part is not decoding the literal sentence. The hard part is asking whether the sender would still want to send that sentence in the state where it is supposed to be truthful.
cheap_talk.course_boundary_note: The boundary is incentive alignment. Cheap talk can transmit information when truthful or partially truthful messages induce receiver actions that the sender is willing to support. It fails when the sender would rather pool states together or always push the receiver in one direction. This is also where the analogy to everyday honesty breaks: the model is not judging moral truthfulness; it is checking whether truth telling survives strategic incentives.

common_knowledge.everyday_problem: The problem is that coordinated action may require more than everyone privately knowing a fact. People may also need to know that others know it, and know that others know that others know it.
common_knowledge.first_principles_reason: Common knowledge exists because higher-order uncertainty can block coordination. A public fact can support behavior that a private fact cannot.
common_knowledge.mathematical_object: The object is an infinite hierarchy: the event is known, everyone knows it is known, everyone knows everyone knows it is known, and so on.
common_knowledge.operation: Start with the event, then ask whether each level of mutual awareness is satisfied. Common knowledge requires the chain not to stop at a finite level.
common_knowledge.worked_mini_example: Suppose a rule change matters only if firms expect rivals to follow it too. If every firm privately receives the rule, each may still wonder whether others received it, whether others know they received it, and whether others know that everyone is reasoning this way. A public announcement does more than deliver information. It creates shared assurance. The common-knowledge ladder explains why the same factual content can have different strategic effects depending on whether it is privately known or publicly known to be shared.
common_knowledge.common_misunderstanding: The mistake is to treat true, known, and common knowledge as the same. They are different levels of shared awareness.
common_knowledge.recognize_in_new_work: Look for coordination failures, public announcements, or arguments that depend on what everyone knows about everyone else's knowledge.
common_knowledge.why_it_matters: Common knowledge matters because coordination can require publicness, not just truth. A fact can be known by everyone individually but still fail to coordinate action if people are unsure whether others know it too.
common_knowledge.what_breaks_without_it: Without common knowledge, the course would miss higher-order uncertainty. Players might all know the same event, yet hesitate because they do not know whether others know, or whether others know that they know.
common_knowledge.naive_problem: A naive approach treats true, known, and publicly known as equivalent. The course separates those levels because strategic coordination can depend on the entire chain of mutual awareness.
common_knowledge.failed_simple_approach: The simple approach fails when private notifications replace public announcements. Each person may have the fact, but not the assurance that others have the same fact and understand that it is shared.
common_knowledge.lecture_emphasis: The common-knowledge lecture makes higher-order belief concrete. The infinite chain sounds abstract, but it explains why public announcements, conventions, and shared rules can change equilibrium behavior.
common_knowledge.cross_course_connections: Common knowledge connects iterated deletion, rationalizability, equilibrium selection, cheap talk, and public communication. It is the knowledge-side analogue of mutual consistency: everyone reasoning must line up at many levels.
common_knowledge.lecture_depth_walkthrough: The lecture-depth version turns a philosophical-sounding infinite chain into a practical coordination object. Knowing a fact is first-order knowledge. Knowing that others know it is a higher level. Knowing that others know that others know it is another level. Strategic action can depend on these levels because each player is choosing partly in response to what they expect others to understand. The transcript anchor that distinguishes mutual knowledge from first- and second-order mutual knowledge is therefore not a side definition. It is the ladder that lets the course explain why public announcements, shared rules, and conventions can support behavior that private information cannot.
common_knowledge.mathematical_intuition: The mathematical intuition is recursive knowledge. Start with an event E. Apply the “everyone knows” operator repeatedly: everyone knows E, everyone knows that everyone knows E, and so on without a finite stopping point.
common_knowledge.student_trap: Students often get stuck because the infinite chain sounds philosophical. The course uses it for concrete coordination: people act differently when a fact is publicly shared than when each person only privately receives it.
common_knowledge.why_math_has_to_exist: The mathematical object has to exist because ordinary language hides the levels. Saying everyone knows can mean many different things: each person separately knows, each knows that the others know, or the fact is public in a way that supports unlimited mutual reasoning. The recursive knowledge notation forces those levels apart. It lets the analyst ask whether a proposed equilibrium relies only on the fact itself or on the public assurance that everyone can reason from the same fact.
common_knowledge.course_boundary_note: The boundary is public assurance. A fact can be true, widely known, and still not common knowledge if players doubt whether others received it, understood it, or recognized that everyone else received it. The model also assumes a level of idealized reasoning that real people may not satisfy. That does not make the concept useless; it tells the reader what kind of coordination failure the concept is isolating.
